standing_rules: A skip is not a success; an empty state is not a clean one; measured zero must look different from never ran.
Never fail-soft a create call; preserve the error envelope.
'Set in the environment' and 'works' are different claims — run check:secrets before blaming code.
Run the SQL with the merge, never after.
An unpriced model id fails loud, never $0.
Trust source, git log, and the tracker over any prose claiming completeness; close items with file:line in the same commit.
Ledger what is unproven — today: the publish->lift loop, and each UI surface until its soak passes.
Closing a task is an act on a verifier's word, never the implementer's. The agent that wrote the code never closes it.
A change to the orchestration tooling is itself ledger work. The machine is not exempt from the discipline it enforces.
Trace a call site to an HTTP route or a cron entry before describing it as live. A correct file:line proves a line exists, not that anything reaches it.

Close an item only when, in the same commit, its box is ticked, the commit body cites the file:line where the change lives, and the acceptance criterion was exercised — run, not read and not reasoned about. If it could not be exercised here, the item is blocked with the reason, never closed.

SURVEY FIRST: the accept's two clauses were already true and already tested — scanRoute.route.test.mjs proves 429 + x-ratelimit-limit 5 + remaining 0 on the 6th request and that the threshold follows SCAN_RATE_LIMIT, over the real POST handler. What was NOT true is that 'one IP' meant an IP. clientBucketKey read x-real-ip first, unconditionally, and x-real-ip is a request header. REPRODUCED against the real module + the real in-memory counter at SCAN_RATE_LIMIT=5: 25 requests with a rotating x-real-ip were allowed 25/25; 25 with a rotating x-forwarded-for were allowed 25/25; and 25 where x-vercel-forwarded-for named ONE client the whole time but x-real-ip rotated were also allowed 25/25. The counter was never wrong, the identity was. FIX (rateLimit.js:73 resolveClientIp): trust ordering, not header ordering. x-vercel-forwarded-for is used first and marked trusted ONLY when VERCEL/VERCEL_URL is set (Vercel strips inbound x-vercel-*; off Vercel that header is as forgeable as any other and is now ignored rather than promoted). SCAN_RATE_LIMIT_IP_HEADER lets a non-Vercel operator declare the header their proxy OVERWRITES. x-real-ip / leftmost x-forwarded-for remain as fallbacks but are reported trusted:false and warn once per process that the limit is bypassable by rotating that header — rule 1: a limit that quietly stops limiting must say so. After the fix all four spoof scenarios give 5 allowed / 20 refused. EXERCISED BY RUNNING, not reading: 33 tests across rateLimit.test.mjs (22, +7), scanRoute.route.test.mjs (7, untouched, still green) and the new scanRateLimitSpoof.route.test.mjs (4) — the last drives the REAL POST /api/scan handler with a trusted address plus two forged ones and asserts which counter moved (trusted 5->6, both forgeries still 5). ZERO VENDOR SPEND: every identity the route could derive — including the shared 'unidentified' bucket — is pre-seeded over the limit before any test runs, so a WRONG implementation still lands on the refusal path. That seed was added after the first negative-control run returned 201 and started an in-memory scan; no credentials are loaded under node --test so nothing was billed, but the hazard is now closed. tasks.title: Three footguns in the rate-limit trust knob
tasks.detail: R0.1.4 closed the spoofable per-IP limit and its verifier found three residual footguns, none defeating the default config but each reachable by an operator. First and worst: SCAN_RATE_LIMIT_IP_HEADER set to host, x-real-ip or x-forwarded-for yields trusted:true AND SUPPRESSES the warn-once, so a bad declaration is strictly worse than leaving the knob unset, which at least warns. The knob does not reject known-forgeable names. Second: VERCEL is tested for presence, so the strings 0 and false are truthy and open the gate — anyone self-hosting who writes VERCEL=0 to mean not-Vercel silently trusts a forgeable header. Third: the knob is undocumented; .env.example lists SCAN_RATE_LIMIT, _WINDOW_MS and _SALT and not this one, so a security-relevant setting whose misuse converts spoofable-and-loud into spoofable-and-silent is documented only in a JSDoc block. Also latent, not live: an IPv6 value carrying a port produces two different buckets with no normalisation, which Vercel does not emit on this header. And nothing corroborates the Vercel-strips-inbound assumption at runtime, so if it were false the envelope would carry trusted:true while staying silent — asserting a confidence never verified.
tasks.accept: A forgeable header name declared in SCAN_RATE_LIMIT_IP_HEADER either is refused or keeps trusted:false and the warning; VERCEL is judged by value rather than presence; and the knob is documented in .env.example with the warning that it must name a header the proxy OVERWRITES. Tests cover the bad-declaration and VERCEL=0 cases.

notes.text: filed mid-rebuild
claimed

All three footguns reproduced against the pre-fix module before I touched it (script output pasted below in the report): SCAN_RATE_LIMIT_IP_HEADER=x-real-ip -> {trusted:true} with ZERO warnings logged; VERCEL='0' -> {trusted:true} on x-vercel-forwarded-for; .env.example had no mention of the knob. Anchors were stale by line number but the code they pointed at is the code I changed (old :73 resolveClientIp, old :79 the VERCEL presence test, .env.example rate-limit block now at :52-80).

CHOICE for the bad declaration: REFUSE the name, do not throw. A refused declaration is dropped, the request falls through to the untrusted fallbacks, so it keeps trusted:false AND trips the existing untrusted-source warning, AND the refusal itself is warned about on its own latch (src/lib/rateLimit.js:318 - separate from warnedUntrustedSource so it can never be swallowed by a warning an earlier request already spent). Measured: unset knob = 1 warning, bad knob = 2 warnings. A bad declaration is strictly LOUDER than no declaration, which is the property the task asks for. I did not throw because a misconfigured trust knob must not take POST /api/scan down - the limit still holds on the fallback identity, exactly where an undeclared deployment already sits. Refused set (src/lib/rateLimit.js:145): host, x-real-ip, x-forwarded-for, x-forwarded-host, forwarded, x-vercel-forwarded-for, each with its reason in the value; plus anything that is not a single RFC 7230 token. x-forwarded-for is refused even though some proxies genuinely overwrite it, because far more APPEND and nothing in the request distinguishes the two while this module reads the leftmost element - reasoned in the comment.

VERCEL by value (src/lib/rateLimit.js:110): 1/true/yes/on open the gate; 0/false/no/off/empty/unset do not; anything else fails CLOSED and warns naming the value, because closed is the safe direction and the operator typed something we cannot honour. VERCEL_URL is a hostname not a flag, so any non-empty value counts EXCEPT the no-words, which are never a hostname and are the same self-hosting mistake.

IPv6 port: HANDLED, not skipped (src/lib/rateLimit.js:202). normaliseAddress strips brackets and a port and case-folds a v6 literal, so [2001:db8::1]:443 and 2001:db8::1 are one bucket. Explicitly NOT full v6 canonicalisation - ::1 vs 0:0:0:0:0:0:0:1 still differ, stated in the comment rather than implied away.

Vercel-strips-inbound: NOT verified and NOT claimed. I added a comment at src/lib/rateLimit.js:74 recording it as an assumption and naming what would actually prove it (an external probe sending a forged x-vercel-forwarded-for at the deployed URL and comparing buckets - a deploy-time check, not something a request handler can see). I added no runtime corroboration, because anything I could add inside the handler would prove nothing.

tasks.title: The perimeter warn-once guard is evadable in one added line
tasks.detail: R0.1.14's verifier evaded its source guard three ways and found it wrong in BOTH directions. Keeping the module-level flag declaration as a decoy and adding the same declaration inside middleware() passes the guard 25 of 25 while the behaviour regresses to one warning per request — the same regression the guard's own sabotage catches when the declaration is MOVED, achieved instead by ADDING. Inserting a single warnedDevOpen.value = false above the call does the same. And renaming the flag to warned with ES2015 shorthand makes the code correct while the guard FAILS. So the guard's assertion message, that the flag must live at module scope or the warning fires every request, asserts something it does not establish. The verifier also rejected the rationale for a source guard: the no-Edge-runtime-here argument is a non-sequitur, because once-ness is a module-scope property observable in plain Node, and this repo already ships the machinery in src/lib/cronAuth.route.hooks.mjs whose own header makes exactly this argument about removing an inference. They wrote a roughly 30-line behavioural test using that unmodified hooks file and Next's real next/server, imported the real middleware, drove 11 requests and asserted one warning: it passes on HEAD, fails on both evasions, and passes on the shorthand shape — correct in all three cases where the source guard is wrong in two.

tasks.title: Nothing proves Vercel strips an inbound x-vercel-forwarded-for
tasks.detail: Filed by the R0.1.18 implementer, who closed the three trust-knob footguns and then declined to claim this one was closed. The rate limiter labels a client IP trusted:true when it comes from x-vercel-forwarded-for on a Vercel deployment. That label rests entirely on the assumption that Vercel's edge OVERWRITES an inbound header of that name rather than passing it through. If the assumption were false, an anonymous request could forge the header, land in an attacker-chosen rate-limit bucket, and the envelope would assert trusted:true while staying completely silent, because the warn-once only fires for UNTRUSTED sources. That is the worst combination: a spoofable identity carrying a confidence label. Nothing inside a request handler can see the difference, so no unit test can settle it; the implementer recorded the assumption in a comment at src/lib/rateLimit.js:74 together with what would actually prove it, and added no runtime corroboration rather than adding a check that proves nothing. The only real proof is external: curl the deployed POST /api/scan with a forged x-vercel-forwarded-for and assert the bucket does not move. This is currently unowned and is the last live hole in the per-IP limit that R0.1.4 and R0.1.18 otherwise closed.
tasks.accept: Either a deploy-time smoke check forges x-vercel-forwarded-for against the deployed origin and asserts the rate-limit bucket does not move, and it runs somewhere an operator sees it; or the trusted:true label is withdrawn from that source until such a check exists. Writing the script without running it is a partial result and must be blocked, not closed.

tasks.title: POST /api/scan returns 201 off a job that only exists in memory
tasks.detail: Identified by the R2.8.6 implementer as the ACTUAL mechanism behind R0.1.4, which the ledger had attributed to insertScan. src/lib/db.js:508-510: createScanJob fail-softs to global.memoryJobs when there is no Supabase client. src/app/api/scan/route.js:57-70 then returns 201 off that in-memory job. So on a deploy with no credentials - or with credentials that stop working - an anonymous request gets a 201 Created and a job id for a scan that was never persisted, and the scan proceeds to spend money on vendor calls whose results have nowhere to land. R0.1.4's negative control hit exactly this: it returned 201 and started an in-memory scan, and nothing was billed only because no credentials load under node --test, which its own author called luck rather than design. R2.8.6 closed the results write; this is the job create, one step earlier, and it never reaches insertScan at all. The memory store is not simply a bug: it is load-bearing for the entire test suite, so removing it needs a decision about whether it is dev-only by assertion rather than dev-only by accident.
tasks.accept: A request cannot receive a 201 for a scan job that was not persisted. Either the route refuses when there is no client, or the memory store is gated behind an explicit development assertion that production cannot satisfy - and the choice is recorded as a decision. A test drives the no-client path against the real route and fails if it returns 201.

tasks.title: The rate limiter warns and continues on a caller-settable client address when off Vercel
tasks.detail: Surfaced by the R0.1.21 implementer while running the scan-route suites, which print a warning that the client address was taken from a header the caller can set and that the per-IP limit is therefore bypassable by rotating it. That is a warn-and-proceed on the money path, in the configuration where the trusted-header env var is unset and the process is not on Vercel. (1) V6, the one this contract's own rule would ACTIVATE: renewBatch is defined and exported in worker/src/lib/queue.js and worker/src/index.js does not import it -- its queue import list is claimBatch, reportBatch, releaseBatch, describeClaim, CLAIM_REASONS -- and git grep renewBatch over worker/ returns only the definition. The document forbids shipping the delays without one of three named fixes.
(2) The thundering herd, derived from three expressions: brightdata backoffMs x attempt (tripled on 429), openai delay(1000 x 2^attempt), perplexity RETRY_BASE_DELAY_MS x 2^attempt -- all deterministic, all per-request, at concurrency 4 or 6. DEFECT 1 — THE SHIPPED MIGRATION STATES THE OPPOSITE OF ITS OWN BEHAVIOUR. supabase/migrations/010_probe_tasks.sql:18-23 reads "LEASE COLUMNS ARE jobLease's COLUMNS ... a NULL owner or a past expiry means free, RE-ACQUIRING YOUR OWN LEASE IS ALLOWED". It is not allowed. That is the deliberate divergence, implemented at :176-178 where the predicate omits jobLease's lease_owner = me clause, self-corrected 150 lines later at :170-175, and proven live at probeTasksRace.test.mjs:263-287. The header carries no hedge, so a reader of the design header alone — the first thing anyone building R1.2.3's reaper will read — is told the exact inverse of the semantics on the subtlest point in the file. FIX: qualify :20-21 to say the predicate is jobLease's MINUS self-reacquisition, and cross-reference the block at :170.

DEFECT 2 — THE EVIDENCE CITATION IS WRONG. probeTasksRace.test.mjs:196 is "await Promise.all(clients.map((c) => c.end()));", connection teardown in the six-workers/six-tasks test. The divergence is asserted at :275 and :282. The other citation, 010_probe_tasks.sql:164, is exactly right.

EVERYTHING ELSE IS VERIFIED — KEEP IT ALL. THE DIVERGENCE ITSELF IS CORRECT: re-handing a worker its own in-flight batch re-runs live probe work with real vendor spend and inflates attempts; jobLease's self-reacquisition exists for idempotent resume of a job whose id the caller already holds, and that rationale does not transfer. The bounded cost is mitigated by release_probe_tasks on a failed pass. "ADOPTS THE EXISTING jobLease PRIMITIVE" IS HONESTLY SATISFIED: TTL matches (LEASE_TTL_MS 180000 equals the SQL default, and probeQueue.test.mjs:441-448 ties the SQL literal to the JS constant so it cannot drift), columns identical, predicate identical minus the documented clause, acquire/renew/release present. The isolation constraint was proven real — adding a jobLease import to worker/src/lib/queue.js makes workerIsolation.test.mjs fail.

CATALOG AUDIT CLEAN: table present with RLS on, three indexes plus pkey, four functions found via pg_proc with SECURITY INVOKER, and ALL FOUR DEPLOYED BODIES BYTE-IDENTICAL to the file. schema_migrations checksum be27ae10f9467429 matches a recomputation from disk under the runner's normalisation. Purely additive — the only ALTER is ENABLE ROW LEVEL SECURITY on its own new table, zero DROP, no FK and zero non-internal triggers on scan_jobs. The no-FK decision is right, but nothing validates scan_job_id at all, so R1.2.3 must own that or orphaned tasks are silently possible.

THE RACE IS GENUINELY CONCURRENT, and the verifier did not take the test's word for it. Holding A's transaction open and observing from a third connection: OBS sees the row as pending/NULL, so B's WHERE clause MATCHES it and the lease predicate cannot be what excludes B; xmax proves A holds the lock; B returned in 155ms without blocking. Only SKIP LOCKED produces that. THE IMPLEMENTER'S OWN WORRY WAS JUSTIFIED AND WORSE THAN STATED: both six-way cases carry NO atomicity teeth at all — they still passed against a function with SKIP LOCKED removed. The deterministic open-transaction case is the entire proof.

TEETH, every sabotage proven by reading prosrc back from pg_proc: plain FOR UPDATE makes B block indefinitely; NO locking clause makes B STEAL THE ROW (lease_owner=B, attempts=2); against a separate teeth function, removing SKIP LOCKED times out the deterministic case, removing the lease predicate fails 5 including "exactly one worker may win; 2 did", and reverting to status = 'pending' fails EXACTLY AND ONLY "an expired lease must be reclaimable". The reclaim fix is correct and guarded twice.

claimBatch REFUSES RATHER THAN RETURNING EMPTY, and the guard has teeth: applying the exact R1.2.1 defeat (if (!client) return new Array()) fails probeQueue.test.mjs while the old regex-style workerIsolation guard passes. Strictly stronger. One wording correction: the commit says workerIsolation "proves the worker stubs by invoking them" plural; it invokes only probeBatch, and claimBatch's coverage moved to probeQueue.test.mjs.

tasks.title: Authenticated ingest POST /api/internal/probe-results
tasks.detail: Worker token, fail-closed, contract-validated against Probe Result Contract v2, idempotent upsert on (job_id, engine, query).
tasks.accept: Unauthenticated POST returns 401; a malformed body returns 422; a repeated valid body produces one row.

notes.text: claimed

BUILT, NOT FIXED. The anchor src/app/api/internal/ DID NOT EXIST at claim time (git ls-files and ls both empty), so there was no finding to reproduce: this is the greenfield ingest route R1.2.4 specifies. Before building I audited the whole /api surface for the security question the task actually asks - a directory named "internal" that only a path name protects - and the answer is that no api/internal/* route existed to be exposed. One route exists now and it is the only member of that directory.

WHAT LANDS. Four new files plus one .env.example entry. (1) src/app/api/internal/probe-results/route.js - POST only, force-dynamic, auth -> parse -> validate -> upsert. (2) src/app/api/internal/_lib/ingestAuth.js - the credential gate. (3) src/app/api/internal/_lib/probeResultContract.js - Probe Result Contract v2 as an executable validator plus the prompt_results mapping. (4) src/lib/probeResultsIngest.route.test.mjs - 28 tests driving the REAL handler. NO MIGRATION: the upsert target is prompt_results and the conflict key (job_id, engine, query) is the UNIQUE constraint migration 005 already declares and prod already has; the test pins both the onConflict string and the SQL constraint so the claim is not prose. Nothing outside src/app/api/internal/**, my test file and .env.example was touched.

ACCEPT, CLAUSE BY CLAUSE, ALL OBSERVED AT THE HANDLER (never inferred from a predicate). (a) Unauthenticated POST returns 401: proven with a VALID body so the 401 cannot be a parse failure wearing an auth badge; with no credential, with a wrong bearer, with a bare "Bearer ", with the right value but no Bearer scheme, with the wrong header name, with x-cron-secret and x-operator-token (this route speaks neither), with ?secret= (not a carrier here - a token in a URL lands in access logs), and with PROBE_INGEST_TOKEN DELETED FROM THE ENVIRONMENT (six shapes including "Bearer undefined" -> all 401). Positive control: the correct token in either header -> 200, so "return 401 always" does not pass. (b) A malformed body returns 422: non-JSON, envelope failures (job_id missing/not-a-uuid, brand missing, results not-an-array/empty), the rejected example from contract section 6.5 with all four independent rejections found by code, and a 32-row table of one-clause-at-a-time mutations so no rejection rides on another. A 422 writes NOTHING - asserted by reading the store back after a batch of one valid plus one invalid row. (c) A repeated valid body produces one row: byte-identical POST twice -> stored:1 twice, store holds 1 row, SAME id; and a different engine on the same query still makes 2 rows, so "one row" cannot be satisfied by a route that drops everything after the first.

FAIL-CLOSED IS STRICTER THAN cronAuth ON PURPOSE. isCronAuthorized allows a missing secret outside production because a Vercel cron and the scan worker self-continue fetch must work on a laptop. This route has neither caller (its only client is worker/, a separate deployment), so an absent PROBE_INGEST_TOKEN denies in EVERY environment including dev, and a blank/whitespace value or one under 24 chars is a misconfiguration that refuses even when the exact value is presented. Comparison is crypto.timingSafeEqual over SHA-256 digests of both sides - equal-length always, so a wrong-length guess is a plain false rather than a throw that leaks the length. The environment is read at REQUEST time, never module scope.

SEVEN SABOTAGES, EXACT COUNTS (baseline for this file: 28 tests / 28 pass / 0 fail). S1 delete the route auth gate -> 22 pass / 6 fail. S2 replace timingSafeMatch with loose == -> 26 pass / 2 fail (constant-time guard plus the call-site guard). S2b replace it with a 4-char prefix compare -> 26 pass / 2 fail (a WRONG credential was accepted: behavioural, not just static). S3 remove both fail-closed branches and make the compare pass when both sides are absent -> 24 pass / 4 fail. S4 point the route walk at a directory that does not exist -> 26 pass / 2 fail, i.e. the enumeration REFUSES rather than going green on nothing. S5 drop the mandatory section-5 "measurement field non-null on a not-measured row" rejection -> 26 pass / 2 fail. S6 store answered=false instead of null for a login_wall row -> 27 pass / 1 fail. S7 make the upsert conflict key unstable -> 27 pass / 1 fail. Every sabotage was reverted from a scratchpad backup and all four files diff CLEAN against it; nobody else file was touched, staged, stashed or reset.

NOT VACUOUS BY CONSTRUCTION. The auth loop never names probe-results: it walks src/app/api/internal/ for every route.js, asserts the walk is non-empty, asserts the discovered set equals EXPECTED_INTERNAL_ROUTES, and then exercises every exported HTTP verb of every discovered route. A route added there tomorrow either fails the member-list assertion (its author has to come here and say what guards it) or is covered automatically. A separate FIXTURE test asserts the two valid rows really are contract-valid, or every 422 above would pass for the wrong reason.

ONE CONTRACT CONTRADICTION, RESOLVED DELIBERATELY AND REPORTED. Sections 3.4 and 5 require every measurement field non-null when state is "answered"; section 6.3 is a worked example the contract calls legitimate with brand_cited and competitors_cited NULL under citations_state "unverified", and section 3.10 exists so that row is representable. Read literally, section 5 rejects section 6.3. I implemented 3.10 as a NARROW exception scoped to exactly those two citation-derived fields and only under "unverified" (tested both ways: 6.3 accepted; widening the nullability to text rejected). The contract document needs the fix - I did not edit docs/contracts/. Corollary I had to decide: with brand_cited unknown and no mention observed, "visible" is not establishable, so that row is rejected (visibility_unestablished) rather than stored as a measured non-mention.

RULE COMPLIANCE. Rule 1: the 200 says WHERE it went (storage: database or process_memory) and warns on the memory path; in production with no Supabase client the batch is 503, never kept in a per-instance Map; an empty results array is 422, never a 200 over zero rows; a short write is 502. Rule 2: upsertPromptResults throws and the route answers 502 with the error message preserved - no catch block can answer with a stored count (asserted). Rule 3: cost.basis "unpriced" with any non-null amount_usd is rejected, "no_charge" must be exactly 0 AND name its rule, and a "ui" row claiming vendor_reported or estimated is rejected because that zero is ours, not the vendor. Rule 4: no migration needed; the constraint relied on is pinned to migration 005 by a test. Rule 5: the stored row writes answered=true for "answered", false ONLY for "no_answer" (the one observed absence), and NULL for the other six states - a login_wall row stored as false is exactly the section-1 failure; an absent is_branded_query stores null, not the column DEFAULT false.

SUITE. npm run test:scoring: 2358 tests, 2331 pass, 1 fail, 26 skipped, exit 0. The single failure is src/lib/workers/scanChunk.test.mjs:494 ("prompt_seeding: null" appearing in a checkpoint stats object) - another agent in-flight work in src/lib/workers/scanWorker.js plus src/lib/scoring/promptGen.js, both on my off-limits list. It fails identically when that file is run alone and cannot be reached by my four new files. Baseline was 2248/2222/0/26; the tree gained 110 tests from concurrent agents plus my 28.

WHAT I DELIBERATELY DID NOT DO, each needing its own task. (1) I did NOT add /api/internal/probe-results to SELF_GATED in src/lib/operatorPerimeter.js. Consequence, stated plainly: in production the operator perimeter also gates this path, so the fleet needs OPERATOR_TOKEN as well as the ingest token to reach the handler. That is defence in depth and safe, but it means the fleet is not deployable against this route until someone decides - and operatorPerimeter.js plus its route-walk guard are outside my allowed paths. (2) I did NOT add PROBE_INGEST_TOKEN to worker/src/config.js or scripts/check-secrets.mjs; worker/ and scripts/ are outside my allowed paths, so the variable is documented in .env.example and unwired on the producer side. (3) NO RATE LIMIT and no body-size limit beyond MAX_RESULTS_PER_BATCH=200; src/lib/rateLimit.js is being changed right now for R0.1.24 so I did not touch it. (4) NO TENANT CHECK: an authenticated caller may write rows for ANY job_id and ANY brand - the route does not verify that job_id exists in scan_jobs or that brand matches that job. With a shared worker token that is inherent rather than a bypass, but a buggy or compromised fleet could poison another tenant scan, and a scan_jobs cross-check would make it fail loud.

WHAT A VERIFIER SHOULD BE MOST SUSPICIOUS OF. (i) The 24-character MIN_TOKEN_LENGTH: a manual curl with a short token gets a 401 that looks like a bug. That is the intended fail-closed behaviour and is tested. (ii) The 3.10 narrowing above - it is the one place I chose between two things the contract says. (iii) The idempotency proof runs through the IN-MEMORY path of upsertPromptResults (Supabase env deleted before import, so the liveWriteGuard preload is never challenged and no live row was written by me). The memory path uses the same job_id|engine|query conflict key, and the live path onConflict string and the migration UNIQUE constraint are pinned by reading source - but the PostgREST upsert itself was NOT executed against a database in this environment, and I am saying so rather than implying otherwise. (iv) The 502 store-failure path is asserted by reading the route source, not by making upsertPromptResults throw; the handler takes no injectable client, which is the same limitation src/lib/db/promptWriteRoute.route.test.mjs records. (v) The api-row cost rule: I read the section-5 "no metered call" bullet as engine_surface === "ui", which is the only machine-checkable reading and is documented at the check.

Dedicated PROBE_INGEST_TOKEN verified with constant-time crypto.timingSafeEqual SHA-256 digests and 24-character floor. Idempotency verified on duplicate delivery. Storage returns documented shape ({ stored, conflict_key, storage }) and fails closed (503/502). All 28 tests in src/lib/probeResultsIngest.route.test.mjs pass. 7 sabotages verified (auth gate, timingSafeMatch, prefix compare, fail-closed removal, missing dir, section-5 drop, unstable conflict key). All 9 citations valid and resolved.

tasks.title: The Bright Data zone cache never invalidates
tasks.detail: resolveBrightDataSerpZone caches the auto-discovered zone in a module-level cachedZoneName with no TTL and no invalidation path. In a request-scoped Vercel function that is harmless, because the module reloads. In the long-lived worker container built by R1.2.1 it is not: a zone that is suspended, deleted or exhausted mid-run keeps being used until someone restarts the process, and every probe then fails for a reason the fleet cannot see. Found while testing R0.1.10, where a no-active-zone fixture silently returned the previous test cached value instead of throwing — the cache is invisible until it misleads you.
tasks.accept: The resolved zone is re-checked at least once per fleet poll cycle, or the cache carries a TTL; a zone that stops being active surfaces as a typed configuration error rather than as N failed probes.

notes.text: filed mid-rebuild
claimed

POLICY: three levers, combined, not one chosen. (1) TTL — cachedZone is now {name, at} (brightdata.js:81) and resolve serves it only while fresh (:145); default 5 minutes (:72), overridable via BRIGHTDATA_ZONE_TTL_MS, 0 = never cache. A malformed TTL throws instead of falling back to the default (:91) — a silent fallback would tell an operator who wrote '30s' that they had a 30s re-check while a dead zone lived on for five minutes. (2) invalidateBrightDataZoneCache() (:116) is exported for the R1.2 fleet to force a re-check per poll cycle; it returns the dropped name, or null when nothing was cached, so 'cleared' and 'was already empty' are different events. (3) Probe-time rejection: zoneRejectionDetail (:291) reads Bright Data's zone refusals out of the HTTP body (:398) and the 200 envelope (:445), zoneRejectedError (:313) drops the cache and returns a typed BrightDataZoneError, and the retry loop refuses to retry one (:478). Recovery is therefore ONE failed probe, not one TTL; the TTL is the backstop for the case Bright Data never tells us about. Per-probe re-listing was rejected on cost: get_all_zones is a real call and that would be ~30 extra per scan. WHY NOT PER-PROBE, WHY BOTH CONSUMERS ARE SERVED: web requests (aioPipeline/enginePipeline) never get to call an invalidator, so they need the clock; a 5-minute TTL is longer than a typical invocation, so their cost profile is unchanged at one lookup per process. The fleet gets the clock AND the explicit invalidator. A re-check that could not be COMPLETED (get_all_zones itself failing) throws lookup_failed and does NOT refresh the timestamp — a grace window serving the stale name through an outage was considered and rejected as exactly the fail-soft this task removes. TYPED, NOT SILENT: BrightDataZoneError carries reason no_active_zone|zone_rejected|lookup_failed|bad_ttl_config, and a re-check that changes nothing logs 'still active' so 'the TTL fired and all is well' cannot be confused with 'the TTL never fired'. R0.1.10 IS NOT REGRESSED: a rejected probe is still an ERROR row and still counted — brightdataZone.test.mjs:334 keeps errored_queries 1 / error_rate_pct 100 and gains an assertion that a PINNED bad zone says it cannot self-heal. THE EXISTING TEST WAS CHANGED, NOT DELETED: brightdataZone.test.mjs:101 'THE BEHAVIOUR CHANGE (R1.2.7)' quotes the old assertions verbatim, keeps them as the within-TTL half (cache still wins, 0 calls), and reverses the second half (expired cache over a suspended-only account throws a typed error and drops the entry). REPRODUCED THEN RECOVERED, mocked fetch only, no live SERP probe: before, a suspended zone gave 3 error rows from 3 wasted SERP calls and 0 lookups; after, 1 SERP call then a typed config error, cache dropped, next resolve follows the account to the new zone. TTL expiry also exercised by the real clock (40ms TTL, 60ms wait), not just the 0 case. TEETH PROVEN by three sabotages against a pristine copy kept outside git (TTL ignored -> 3 fails; rejection no longer drops the cache -> 1 fail; silent TTL fallback -> 1 fail), each restored and diffed identical. check-secrets cold-cache tests still pass (9/9 across checkSecretsBrightdata.test.mjs + checkSecretsBrightdataNoZone.test.mjs); I made COMMENT-ONLY edits in those two files because their prose asserted 'module-level with no invalidator ... wins forever', which my change makes false — the process-isolation rationale is retained and restated, no assertions touched. Suite: 1128 tests, 1109 pass, 0 fail, 19 skipped (baseline 1106/1087/0/19; the extra tests are mine plus other lanes' concurrent work). NOT DONE, needs its own task: (a) scripts/check-secrets.mjs still tells the operator the zone is cached 'for the process lifetime' (the PASS detail string and the comment above it) — now overstated, and outside my allowed file set; (b) docs/vendors/brightdata.md:73-87 documents the old no-invalidator behaviour and cites brightdataZone.test.mjs:71-82; (c) the worker cannot import src/ by design (workerIsolation guard), so nothing calls invalidateBrightDataZoneCache() per poll cycle yet — the TTL is what satisfies the accept today.

verification.note:
VERIFIED. THE STALE CACHE REPRODUCED with a mocked fetch and the zone suspended mid-run: pre-fix, 3 wasted SERP calls, 3 error rows, errored_queries 3 and error_rate_pct 100, and the resolver returned the dead zone FOREVER. Post-fix the same fixture gives one typed BrightDataZoneError on probe 1 then self-heals — probes 2 and 3 succeed on the new zone at real cost, errored_queries 1, error_rate_pct 33.3. Recovery is one failed probe, not one TTL, exactly as claimed.

THE TTL IS PROVEN BY WALL CLOCK, not the TTL=0 special case: two resolves inside a 40ms window keep the call count at 1, a real 60ms wait, then the account swaps and the resolver follows. AND IT IS NOT FLAKY — 88 runs, zero failures, including 48 concurrent on 12 cores at 4x oversubscription. The only theoretical window is a >40ms preemption between two consecutive resolves; the 60ms wait cannot flake the other way since setTimeout is a floor.

THE 200-ENVELOPE PATH IS GENUINELY REACHED, driven directly rather than read: both an ok:true body carrying "zone not found" and a status:error message form classify as zone_rejected. Rate-limit precedence holds on that path, with quota and 429 wordings still classified as rate limit. THE VERIFIER FOUND AN ASYMMETRY THE NOTE DID NOT CLAIM: precedence does NOT exist on the !res.ok path, where zoneRejectionDetail runs first, so an HTTP 429 whose body says "zone quota expired" is typed as a zone rejection and not retried where the pre-fix code retried with backoff. Contrived wording, the row still errors and counts, so not fail-worthy — but the symmetry is looser than stated. False negatives are also internally inconsistent: snake_case forms like zone_suspended fall through to a plain Error because two patterns need a word boundary that underscore cannot provide. Cost is bounded: it degrades to the TTL, slower recovery, never silent success.

THE FAIL-LOUD LOOKUP BRANCH IS MILDER THAN SUPPOSED AND THE VERIFIER AGREES WITH IT: getBrightDataConfig is called OUTSIDE the retry loop, so a control-plane outage lands in enginePipeline's per-query catch and produces N loud counted error rows — identical to what pre-fix did on a cold cache, with no fabricated clean state. The cache is retained and its timestamp not refreshed, so the re-check succeeds once the outage ends. The grace-window alternative could not distinguish "control plane down, zone fine" from "control plane down, zone dead".

THREE CLAIMED SABOTAGES REPRODUCE EXACTLY 3/1/1, each diffed against a pristine copy outside git and restored byte-identical. THE VERIFIER ADDED A FOURTH AND FOUND THE ONE GAP: deleting the 200-envelope check leaves the suite FULLY GREEN, because both zone-rejection tests use ok:false and nothing pins the envelope. The branch works — proven manually — but is unprotected against the next editor. Not a fail: the accept is met via the HTTP path and deleting it degrades to the TTL rather than to a false success. Filed as the next task.

R0.1.10 HAS NOT REGRESSED: 9/9 across both cold-cache files, with the diff on them verified line by line as comment-only and no assertion touched. The probe-time error state holds — row.error set, answer_present false, errored_queries 1 — never a skip with a clean cost 0.0.

TEST-ORDER COUPLING BREAKS LOUDLY, NEVER VACUOUSLY: each order-dependent test opens by asserting the state it inherits, so running one in isolation fails on that line rather than passing on an empty cache. Documented in the file header. And the rewritten test is honest — the verifier pulled the pre-fix version and compared: the comment quotes the old name and both old assertions character for character, the fixture is preserved identically, and the test is NAMED "THE BEHAVIOUR CHANGE". Not a quiet swap.

All 8 citations resolve exactly. invalidateBrightDataZoneCache has no production consumer yet, which the note states honestly; the TTL branch is independently live through POST /api/scan to runScanChunk to enginePipeline to brightDataSearch. CORRECTION TO MY BRIEF: the baseline of 1109 already counted this commit; the true figure at ef9909b is 1104, and post-fix is 1109, exactly +5 for the 5 new tests.

tasks.title: The six-way race tests pass with SKIP LOCKED removed
tasks.detail: R1.2.2's two six-worker cases in src/lib/probeTasksRace.test.mjs carry NO atomicity teeth: its verifier ran them against a claim function with FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED stripped and both still passed. Real concurrency on a small local pool tends to serialize, so the racers arrive in sequence and each correctly finds the previous claim, which looks like a win. The entire proof of atomicity is the one deterministic case that holds worker A's transaction open from a third connection while B tries — that case does fail when SKIP LOCKED is removed (B blocks indefinitely) and when the locking clause goes entirely (B steals the row). Before real concurrent workers hit this in R1.2.4, the six-way cases should either be hardened so they genuinely contend, or relabelled as smoke coverage so nobody mistakes them for the atomicity proof they are not.
tasks.accept: Removing FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED from the claim function fails at least one six-way race test, or those tests are renamed and commented to state they do not prove atomicity and to point at the deterministic case that does.

notes.text: filed mid-rebuild
claimed

CHOICE OF APPROACH: (b) static SQL-text assertion, stated as such in the new file's header.  1. FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED deleted from the candidate CTE (line 183) -> probeClaimLock.test.mjs 3 pass / 3 FAIL.

verification.note: PASS on the accept's SECOND branch, taken honestly. The first branch (make the six-way race tests fail without SKIP LOCKED) cannot be met with no Postgres here, and the implementer did not claim it was. Verifier reproduced the toothlessness: with the executable clause deleted from 010_probe_tasks.sql:183, probeQueue.test.mjs stays 25/25 GREEN while the new probeClaimLock guard goes 3 pass / 3 FAIL. A bare FOR UPDATE also gives 3/3 with a DISTINCT diagnosis naming the blocking-not-skipping behaviour, so the two bugs are told apart. The reasoning holds on inspection - statement_timeout does cover time waiting on a row lock, connect() builds a fresh unpooled client per test so the SET is session-scoped, and the /statement timeout/i matcher at :271 would catch the abort - but it remains unexecuted until someone runs test:live. FOLLOW-UP, redundancy not coverage: the CTE scoping works (attack 3 went red) but nothing pins it - replacing candidateCte's body with a passthrough leaves the guard 6/6 green, so a future refactor could quietly retire the scoping. Filed as R1.2.15.

tasks.title: promptGen swallows a PAA failure with no log at all
tasks.detail: Proven by execution during R1.2.9, and worse than the rejection that prompted the look. When a typed BrightDataZoneError reaches promptGen directly there is NO throw and NO LOG LINE: promptGen.js:222-224 is a bare catch around the paaFn/autoFn race at :212. The console.warn at :266-268 that a reader might mistake for the net belongs to a CONDITIONAL realism blend gated at :259 and never fires on this path. So the outer net is quieter than the inner one — serp.js:352 at least warns once and drops the cache before returning an empty list. The consequence is that a dead Bright Data zone during sourcing produces a scan whose prompt set was seeded from nothing, with no evidence anywhere that seeding was attempted and failed. Standing rule 1: a skip is not a success. Note R3.7.4 already rethreaded ONE path through here — a policy refusal now rethrows from promptGen.js:176 rather than becoming an empty snippet — so the precedent for making this loud exists in the same function. R3.7.6 covers the leaked timer in the same file and could be done in one pass. rebuild-implementer addendum (three fragments of the submit note were eaten by shell backtick expansion, restored here): (a) "promptGen builds a SEEDING record" — the local const is named seeding, promptGen.js:330. (b) Teeth part one: reverting the serp.js zone rethrow by changing the guard at serp.js:365 to if (false) turns 1 test red (fetchPeopleAlsoAsk propagates a typed zone error). (c) Teeth part two: commenting out the assignment stats.prompt_seeding = seeding at promptGen.js:501 turns 7 tests red. Both reverts were undone and the files byte-verified against a pre-teeth copy before submit.
tasks.accept: A PAA or autocomplete seeding failure is visible to the caller rather than swallowed: either it propagates, or it is recorded where the scan can see it, and a bare catch with no log remains nowhere on that path. A test drives a typed zone error into prompt generation and fails if nothing is emitted.

tasks.title: The perplexity retry guard is dead code, so a 401 costs three calls and three seconds
tasks.detail: Reported by the R2.2.2 implementer and out of scope there. The status check guarding retry in probeAnswer and probeSearch is dead: the throw below it is caught by the enclosing catch, which backs off and retries regardless of status. So a 401 from a bad or revoked key is retried three times with backoff before failing. Not a false success - the failure is real and typed - but it triples the latency and the call count on the one error an operator most needs to see quickly. TEETH PROVEN (the previous note lost a shell-mangled fragment): the line I temporarily deleted on disk is the early-exit guard inside withRetry at src/lib/engines/perplexity.js:218, which breaks the retry loop when isRetryableFailure(e) is false. With it deleted, perplexity.test.mjs:395, :427 and :459 failed with actual 3 / expected 1 and their durations went from ~2ms to ~3020ms; the file was then restored byte-identical from a scratchpad copy (diff -q clean) before submit.

What it buys is that the silent direction stays impossible: 41 non-test source lines across 19 files carry a '//' inside a string literal, and the day one of them precedes an import the naive stripper would delete a live edge and quietly shrink the graph. tasks.title: insertScan cascade 3 writes the row and reports failure, so a re-finalize inserts a duplicate
tasks.detail: Found by the R2.8.6 implementer while making insertScan fail loud, and flagged in a doc comment rather than silently fixed because it changes the wire shape. src/lib/db.js:249-251, the third and last cascade, performs its insert WITHOUT a .select(). PostgREST resolves data: null on SUCCESS in that case. So insertScan returns null for a row that WAS written. runFinalizePhase then reports 'Failed to save scan results', the job is marked failed, and no scan_id is stamped on the checkpoint. A re-finalize therefore finds no stamped scan_id and inserts a SECOND scans row for the same scan. This is the exact mirror of the finding R2.8.6 closes: that one was a create that reported nothing on failure, this one is a create that reports failure on success, and the consequence is worse because it is silent duplication of customer rows rather than a loud refusal. It also interacts badly with R2.8.6's new throw: the throw makes the failure path more reachable, so the duplicate-row path becomes more reachable too, not less. TWO CORRECTIONS from the R2.8.6 verifier, which confirmed the bug at the library level and empirically. CONFIRMED: postgrest-js dist/index.mjs:614 shows .select() is the ONLY thing that appends Prefer: return=representation, and :378-385 shows processResponse initialises data to null and, on a 201 with an empty body, hits an EMPTY BLOCK - so data stays null and error stays null. db.js:247-252: cascades 1 and 2 call .select(), cascade 3 does not. Driven with a stub forcing cascades 1 and 2 to error: 3 attempts, insertScan returned null, caller read null, for a row that WAS written. CORRECTION 1 - R2.8.6 did NOT make this more reachable. Its diff touches cascade 3 only to swap the module binding for the resolved client and to wrap the ERROR path; the cascade-3 SUCCESS path is byte-for-byte identical before and after. CORRECTION 2 - the duplicate-row consequence is NARROWER than filed. runScanChunk at scanWorker.js:2069 returns already_finished for a job whose status is complete or failed, and shouldRescueJob at :845 returns false for failed, so the cron resume sweep will not re-finalize a falsely-failed job. A duplicate requires the outer catch's own updateScanJob to ALSO fail (leaving the job in scoring with a stale heartbeat, then rescued) or a manual re-dispatch. THE ROUTINE OUTCOME, which is what this task should be scoped to fix, is an ORPHANED scans ROW PLUS A JOB THAT LIES ABOUT FAILING: no prompt_results.scan_id, no citations, no result_brands, no brand_metrics_daily rollup, and a failed job the customer sees for a scan that actually succeeded. tasks.title: The content event and lease writers take no deps and swallow their own errors
tasks.detail: Found by the R3.2.4 author while closing the live-write adoption gap, and stated as the reason two of the seven offender test files could not simply be fixed by injection. src/lib/db.js:668 - insertContentEvent catches its own error and falls back to memory, and getContentEvents is the same shape; neither takes a deps argument, so a test cannot inject a client and is forced to manipulate ambient environment instead. src/lib/content/contentWorker.js passes no deps to acquireLease, renewLease or releaseLease for the same reason. The consequence the live write guard exposed: contentLift.test.mjs called the real insertContentEvent, the guard REFUSED the production write, and the test still passed - because the function swallowed the refusal and fell back to memory. Which means the symmetric case is also true and is the real finding: without the guard, a SUCCESSFUL production write from a test would have been equally invisible. A create that swallows its own failure cannot tell anyone whether it wrote, and that is the same class as R2.8.4 on the read side and R2.8.6 on the scans create. SCOPE WIDENED by the R2.2.3 audit, which enumerated all 35 write helpers under src/lib/db. This finding is not two functions, it is ELEVEN of the same shape plus two variants. In src/lib/db/content.js and src/lib/db/knowledge.js: insertContentItem, insertContentFeedback, upsertBrandBrief, insertLessons, setLessonActive, insertAgent, updateAgent, deleteAgent, insertKnowledgeBlock, updateKnowledgeBlock and deleteKnowledgeBlock each do catch(err){ console.warn; write to a global memory map; return the record }. A REFUSED production write and a SUCCESSFUL one return the same shaped record and the caller cannot tell them apart - which is exactly how the live write guard found contentLift.test.mjs passing while its write was being refused. Each has one real call site. TWO VARIANTS worth naming separately: deleteAgent and deleteKnowledgeBlock collapse 'no client', 'database error' and 'no such row' into a bare false - the identical bug R2.2.3 just fixed in updatePromptStatus, where the route mapped false to a 404 and told the user their record did not exist during an outage. Check those two call sites for the same lie. Also confirmed CLEAN by the same audit and needing no work: every helper in src/lib/db/analytics.js throws on error; recordCronTick is a deliberate documented fail-soft whose success and failure ARE distinguishable by return value; src/lib/scanRuns.js and src/lib/probeQueue.js route every PostgREST error through a throwDbError helper that preserves the envelope. Separately, the R3.2.4 author notes the uninjectability is the other half of this: contentWorker.js passes no deps to acquireLease/renewLease/releaseLease and insertContentEvent/getContentEvents take none, so five offender tests can only work around it by deleting env vars before a dynamic import - an order-sensitive pattern currently held up by a supabase===null tripwire in each file. CORRECTION from the R2.2.3 verifier, which checked the delete helpers itself rather than accepting the audit. deleteAgent and deleteKnowledgeBlock do NOT collapse no-such-row into false, as the previous amendment said. src/lib/db/content.js:836 and src/lib/db/knowledge.js:103 issue a delete().eq('id', id) with NO .select() and NO row-count check, so deleting a NONEXISTENT id RETURNS TRUE - a fabricated success, which is worse than the miscategorised failure. Only the no-client and database-error cases return false. So these two helpers get it wrong in both directions at once: a real outage reads as a missing row, and a missing row reads as a completed deletion. Also corrected: the 'eleven helpers of the memory-fallback shape' figure is unverified - the verifier counts 16 write helpers across content.js and knowledge.js, of which 6 have a clear error-to-memory return. And the audit's '35 write helpers under src/lib/db' is 27 by direct insert/upsert/update/delete call, a definitional difference rather than a substantive one. The class and the remedy are unchanged; the counts and the delete-helper behaviour in this brief are now the verified ones.
tasks.accept: insertContentEvent, getContentEvents and the three lease functions accept injectable deps and report a write failure rather than swallowing it into a memory fallback; a test can drive them with a fake client and no ambient environment. A test fails if a refused or failed write is reported as success.

tasks.title: insertScan cascades 1 and 2 can retry an already-written row into a duplicate
tasks.detail: Found by the R2.8.7 implementer while fixing the same blind spot in cascade 3, and deliberately left alone because it is the path production actually uses. Cascades 1 and 2 do call .select(), so they normally get their row back. But if a proxy ever stripped the Prefer header, PostgREST would resolve {data: null, error: null} on the MODERN schema and produce the identical orphan R2.8.7 just closed for the legacy one. The dangerous part is that the obvious fix is wrong: dropping confirmScanWritten into cascade 1 or 2's try block would have the throw caught by that cascade's OWN catch, which then falls through to the next cascade and INSERTS A SECOND ROW. So an unconfirmed write would become a guaranteed duplicate. It needs abort-not-retry semantics - the catches at src/lib/db.js:229 and :244 must rethrow a ScanWriteError untouched rather than treating it as a reason to try the next shape, exactly as cascade 3's catch now does at :275. This must land in the same change as any confirmation added to those cascades, never before it.
tasks.accept: An unconfirmable write on cascade 1 or 2 aborts with the unconfirmed code rather than falling through to the next cascade, so a written row is never followed by a second insert. A test drives a cascade-1 insert that returns no representation and fails if a second insert is attempted or if the failure is relabelled as nothing-was-stored.

tasks.title: runFinalizePhase flattens the write-error code into prose, so an operator cannot branch on it
tasks.detail: Found by the R2.8.7 implementer. R2.8.6 introduced a discriminated failure on insertScan - db_not_configured means fix the environment, db_write_failed means the database rejected it - and R2.8.7 added a third, db_write_unconfirmed, which means a scans row MAY ALREADY EXIST and the operator must look before re-running. All three are lost at the same place: src/lib/workers/scanWorker.js:1892-1894 builds the string 'Failed to save scan results: ' plus insertErr.message and drops err.code entirely. That string is what lands in scan_jobs.error_message and it is the only thing an operator reading a failed job sees. So the distinction the two previous tasks were built to create never reaches the person who needs it, and the most consequential of the three - go look, you may have an orphaned row - is indistinguishable from nothing happened. The operator's next action differs in each case, which is the whole point of a discriminated failure.
tasks.accept: The write-error code survives to scan_jobs.error_message or to a sibling column, so an operator can tell a misconfiguration from a rejection from an unconfirmed write without parsing prose. A test drives each of the three codes through runFinalizePhase and fails if they are indistinguishable on the job row.

This is the same field R2.7.16 defended one layer down, and its consumer-side fix cannot detect this one because by then it is a genuine 0. :969 is the field the sweep was already told to inspect and it is fed from here. (2) :1614-1626 and :1656/:1659/:1662 - || 0 and : 0 on persisted metrics in the scan-level mirror. :1626 is error_rate_pct: aioSummary.error_rate_pct || 0, the scan-level twin of the same field, and per the comment at :1629-1632 it is written straight onto the persisted scans row by scanWorker.js, so this one reaches the database and not just the screen. Do not treat this list as complete; it is a head start on the enumeration.

tasks.title: The scan worker route reports processed:1 for a request that failed
tasks.detail:
GET /api/scan/worker with a garbage job_id returns HTTP 200 with {processed: 1}. getScanJob throws on a non-uuid, runScanChunk returns {ok:false, reason:read_failed}, and src/app/api/scan/worker/route.js:61 reports processed:1 regardless of what runScanChunk returned. This is a false success on a route the cron drives every day, so a chunk that did nothing is indistinguishable in the response from one that worked. Found by the R3.2.1 implementer, whose change now makes the failure VISIBLE in the scan_runs ledger — a failed row with reason read_failed — but the route response is still wrong and was outside that accept. Standing rule 1: a skip is not a success. NOTE CORRECTION (the submit note above lost every backtick-quoted word to shell substitution; this is the intended text, complete).

REPRODUCED FIRST, then fixed, then proved the teeth.

REPRO (run, not read): the new suite against the PRISTINE pre-fix route (git show HEAD:...route.js, kept outside git in the scratchpad) fails 6/9 with the production body verbatim: {"processed":1,"job_id":"not-a-real-job-id-<emoji>","mode":"direct-resume"} at HTTP 200 — and the same {processed:1, HTTP 200} for a chunk whose job read THREW (read_failed).

THE FIX. route.js:79 classifyChunkResult delegates to scanWorker's exported pure chunkRunOutcome — the same function that writes the scan_runs row — so wire and ledger cannot disagree about one execution, and a reason added to runScanChunk later lands in exactly one place. Ledger outcome -> wire bucket: succeeded (complete, checkpointed) -> processed; skipped (not_found, sourcing_claimed_elsewhere, finalize_claimed_elsewhere) -> skipped; noop (already_finished, noop_status_*) -> skipped; failed (read_failed, chunk_failed, unmapped_chunk_reason:*) -> failed; anything else -> failed. checkpointed counts as processed because the CHUNK worked (probed, checkpointed, handed off) even though the JOB is unfinished. noop and skipped both mean 'this chunk performed no work' on the wire, and the ledger reason travels in the reason field so the ledger's noop/skipped distinction is not lost. route.js:92 is belt and braces on the accept sentence: a result with ok !== true can never leave as processed even if the mapping changed — it becomes failed with reason inconsistent_ok_false:<x>. chunkRunOutcome(undefined) is already failed/unmapped, so a runScanChunk that returns nothing fails loud.

BODY (route.js:104): {mode, job_id, outcome, reason, ledger_outcome, processed, skipped, failed} — explicit 0/1 counters, so a measured zero is visible rather than absent.

STATUS CODE, deliberate: processed and skipped are 200 (an absent job, an already-finished job, or a claim lost to a concurrent invocation are normal; 5xx there pages someone for nothing). failed is 500 (route.js:160). Justification: it is the same class of event as the exception path below it, and since R3.2.1 made openScanRun throw on a total DB outage, that outage now surfaces EITHER as an exception (500) or, when only the job read fails, as read_failed — making read_failed a 200 would let severity depend on which internal call happened to throw. Both 500 bodies now carry the same counters (route.js:166-178). Nothing retries on it: defaultSelfContinue in scanWorker.js is fire-and-forget and never reads the response, and vercel.json's cron calls /api/scan/worker with NO job_id, so the daily cron never touches this branch.

BOTH PATHS. There is no ?batch=1 on this route — that is /api/content/worker; the scan worker's second path is the sweep. Sweep (route.js:249) now reports {mode:sweep, dispatched, job_ids, active, scheduled, scheduler_ok, scheduler_error}: dispatched, not processed, because it fires chunks and never awaits them, so it is in no position to report an outcome (each chunk files its own scan_runs row); active makes an idle tick legible — 0 active and 0 dispatched is a healthy quiet day, no longer identical to 20 active jobs none of which we kicked. A failed scheduler tick used to leave scheduled:[], the same answer as 'nothing was due'; it is now scheduled:null plus scheduler_ok:false plus scheduler_error, still HTTP 200 because the sweep itself succeeded. The no-Supabase early return (route.js:187) says mode:no-db, dispatched:0 and keeps its 200, so cronAuth.route.test.mjs's positive controls still pass.

EXERCISED, not inferred. New suite src/lib/scanWorkerRoute.route.test.mjs drives the REAL GET handler through cronAuth.route.hooks.mjs (nothing stubbed); 9/9 pass. Observed responses: garbage job_id -> 200 outcome:skipped reason:not_found processed:0; getScanJob throwing (global.memoryJobs swapped for a store whose get() throws — the code under test untouched, only its data source fails) -> 500 outcome:failed reason:read_failed processed:0; already_finished (ok is TRUE here, so 'count ok:true as processed' would still fail) -> 200 skipped; noop_status_awaiting_review -> 200 skipped; no job_id -> 200 with no processed key at all. NO SCAN IS STARTED: Supabase env cleared before import, every job_id returns before a work phase, sweep returns at the no-Supabase guard. The sweep body itself was exercised in a scratchpad probe against a fake local PostgREST answering [] — 200 {mode:sweep,dispatched:0,job_ids:[],active:0,scheduled:[],scheduler_ok:true,scheduler_error:null} — and with the scan_schedules select 500ing — 200 {...,scheduled:null,scheduler_ok:false,scheduler_error:'schedules table exploded'}. That probe is not committed.

NOT DRIVABLE HERE, stated in the suite header rather than papered over: the processed bucket itself. complete and checkpointed both need a real probing/finalize phase, i.e. real Bright Data and LLM spend. Covered at two removes: MAPPING tests assert chunkRunOutcome directly across the whole vocabulary, and a source GUARD pins SUCCEEDED -> processed.

TEETH, against a pristine copy kept outside git. (1) Full revert to the unconditional count: 6/9 fail, quoting the production body. (2) Surgical: the processed ternary replaced by the literal 1 — 4 route tests fail. (3) failed answering 200 instead of 500 — the read_failed test fails. tasks.title: The content worker sweep counts dispatched as done, and an in-memory scan leaves no ledger row
tasks.detail: Two findings from the R3.1.3 implementer, who fixed the scan worker route and could not reach these. First: /api/content/worker has the same dispatched-counted-as-done shape the scan sweep had. Its route reports the batch honestly but the resume count less so, and it is the route with the real ?batch=1 which R3.1.3 deliberately did not touch. Now that the scan worker route has set the vocabulary — processed, skipped and failed as explicit counters, with the ledger reason travelling on the wire — the content worker should follow it rather than diverge. Second, and the sharper one: the !ledger.enabled path in scanWorker.js writes NO scan_runs row at all in in-memory mode. It warns loudly, but an operator running with Supabase misconfigured gets a 200 sweep and an empty ledger, which is precisely never-ran wearing the face of a measured zero — the ledger says nothing happened and the response says everything is fine. That is standing rule 1 against the very table R3.2.1 built to close it.
tasks.accept: The content worker sweep distinguishes dispatched from completed the way /api/scan/worker now does. A chunk that runs in in-memory mode either records a run row marked as such, or the sweep response says plainly that no ledger is being written, so an empty ledger can never be mistaken for an idle system.

tasks.detail: Found by the R1.1.3 scribe. git grep waitUntil over src/ and package.json returns NOTHING, and @vercel/functions is not a dependency. tasks.title: recordCronTick fabricates liveness in an unconfigured deploy, so health shows a fresh tick while the cron answers 500
tasks.detail: Found by the R2.8.14 verifier. src/lib/db/analytics.js:555-561 - with no supabase client, recordCronTick writes the tick into global.memorySystemHeartbeats, and getCronTicks at :571-573 reads that same in-memory map straight back. So /api/health in a misconfigured deploy can display a fresh content-worker tick while the cron itself is correctly answering HTTP 500. This is the exact defect R2.8.14 just fixed, one surface over, and it is worse here because it actively contradicts the fix: R2.8.14 made the cron tell the truth about an outage and the health endpoint goes on reporting that the cron ran. An operator triaging a stalled queue will look at health first and be told everything is fine. In-memory state in a serverless deployment also does not survive between invocations or across instances, so the tick is not even a reliable local signal.
tasks.accept: A cron tick recorded with no data store is not readable back as a measured tick. Either recordCronTick refuses and the health endpoint reports the liveness of that cron as unknown rather than fresh, or the tick carries an explicit unmeasured/in-memory state that /api/health renders as such - never as a timestamp that reads like a real one. A missing tick and an unstored tick must stay distinguishable from a genuinely recent tick. A test drives the health endpoint with no supabase configured and asserts no cron reports as fresh, plus a positive case where a genuinely stored tick still reports fresh. Teeth proven by restoring the in-memory read and watching the test go red.

tasks.title: A lease-acquire failure is indistinguishable from a lease legitimately held, and a batch job whose dispatch fails vanishes from every counter
tasks.detail: Two findings from the R3.1.4 verifier, both in src/app/api/content/worker/route.js, both left standing by the task that imported the honest-counter vocabulary. FIRST: dispatchWithLease at route.js:51-64 returns null both when another worker legitimately holds the lease - benign, expected, the system working - and when acquireLease THROWS, which is a data-store failure. The route folds both into skippedIds and answers HTTP 200. So a lease-table outage is reported to the cron as skipped:N with a success status: could not look disguised as chose not to, which is the fail-quiet class R2.8.14 was filed for. The R3.1.4 detail explicitly asked for the ledger reason to travel on the wire and it does not. The error side is untested. SECOND: route.js:243-244 reads const owner = await dispatchWithLease(job.id, batch job); if (owner) batchCreated.push(job.id); with no else. A batch job that is created in content_jobs but whose dispatch fails appears in neither batch_dispatched nor batch_failed - it is silently dropped from BOTH tallies, so the sweep response does not add up. Pre-existing rather than introduced, and the next resume sweep does recover the job, but an unreconciled counter is how a stalled queue stays invisible. THIRD, cheap and adjacent: route.js:185 and contentWorkerSweep.route.test.mjs:98 both say ledger_written:false means no scan_runs row was recorded. The content cron never writes scan_runs; its ledger is content_runs. The field behaves correctly, the prose names the wrong table.
tasks.accept: skipped carries a reason so a lease legitimately held is distinguishable on the wire from a lease acquire that failed, and a lease-store failure does not reach the caller as HTTP 200 - it goes through the same batch_unavailable path R2.8.14 established rather than inventing a second shape. Every created batch job lands in exactly one counter, so dispatched plus failed plus skipped reconciles against created, asserted by a test. REPRODUCED FIRST, at the route: driving the REAL exported GET in-process with a constructed Request against the REAL supabase-js client (fetch answering PostgREST JSON for a host that does not resolve), the old route made EXACTLY ONE DB call - GET /rest/v1/scan_jobs - and answered {status:"probing",progress_pct:62}. It answered byte-identically whether a chunk was beating 5s ago, or the last chunk had closed FAILED 20 minutes earlier with probes_attempted 12 / probes_succeeded 0 / errors_recovered 3, or nothing had ever run. scan_runs was never touched, so migration 011's scan_runs_job_idx - whose own comment names this read as R3.2.3's - had no reader. The rescue was decided by shouldRescueJob(job) reading scan_jobs.heartbeat_at, and its verdict never reached the client.

FIX (route.js only, +461/-3): readRunHistory (:341, SELECT at :357) reads scan_runs by scan_job_id ordered started_at DESC with limit RUN_HISTORY_LIMIT+1 - the index's exact shape, and the +1 so truncated is MEASURED. summarizeRuns (:179) is a pure classifier over the rows. decideRescue (:294) replaces the heartbeat guess. The response carries an execution block (:494) with the recent runs, the open run, outcomes, reasons and counters.

FIVE STATES, NOT ONE. running = an open row beating inside HEARTBEAT_STALE_MS. stalled = an open row whose writer stopped beating (the row R3.3.2 reaps). idle = read succeeded, all rows closed. never_ran = read succeeded, ZERO rows: runs [] and runs_returned 0, a measured zero. unknown = the ledger could not be read: runs null NOT [], runs_returned null NOT 0, truncated null NOT false, with unknown_reason one of no_database_configured | read_failed | row_unreadable | open_run_heartbeat_unreadable and the database's own message in unknown_detail. A failed scan_runs read does NOT downgrade the job reading into the transient envelope (the job row WAS read), so a real status/progress reading is never thrown away by the client.

TIMING DELIBERATELY UNCHANGED, EVIDENCE CHANGED. "Is an executor alive" now comes from the ledger; "how long before kicking an idle job" stays a HEARTBEAT_STALE_MS debounce measured from the newest ledger sign of life (or job.created_at when nothing has ever run, which is exactly what createScanJob's creation-time heartbeat stamp did under the old rule). So a just-checkpointed job is not kicked on every 2s poll (reason recent_sign_of_life) and a dead one is (no_live_executor). Every non-firing path names itself in execution.rescue.reason.

ORPHAN CASE, found by attacking my own first draft (:270): after a successful rescue the ledger holds a stale OPEN row from the chunk that died PLUS a newer closed row from its replacement, and that state persists for minutes until the reaper's 2 x TTL. Reporting it "stalled" would name a dead predecessor as the present, so an open row superseded by a later close is reported executor idle with open_run_orphaned true - visible, not hidden, and not the job's state. Liveness also picks the open row with the FRESHEST beat, not the newest started_at.

tasks.title: A live test wrote to production because only its reads were stubbed
tasks.detail: While building R3.2.1, an earlier draft of its live test stubbed only the READ side of the chunk. The chunk therefore ran through to finalize and the real insertScan wrote 2 rows into scans plus 2 into brand_metrics_daily on the production database. The implementer self-reported it, deleted exactly those four rows in one transaction, and verified restoration; the controller independently confirmed the counts before committing (scans 60, brand_metrics_daily 46, scan_jobs 80, prompt_results 1070, citations 6631, result_brands 2822, newest scan still 2026-07-30). No customer data was lost and nothing was overwritten. The live file now stubs every finalize and sourcing write behind an assert.fail guard, but that guard is a convention the next author has to remember rather than a property of the harness. Two other live-test authors this session came close to the same edge: R0.1.4's negative control returned 201 and started an in-memory scan, saved only by no credentials being loaded under node --test, which its author called luck rather than design. The pattern is that a live-DB test harness that stubs reads looks finished, and the write path only announces itself by writing.
tasks.accept: A live test cannot reach a production write by omission: the harness refuses writes by default and a test must opt in explicitly per table, so a newly added live test that forgets to stub a writer fails loudly rather than writing. Proven by writing a test that omits a stub and watching it fail.

New harness module src/lib/liveWriteGuard.js: default-deny write guard for live-DB tests, opt-in per table. Two choke points, both patched at the PROTOTYPE so they cover clients created before and after install: (1) SupabaseClient.prototype.from/rpc/schema, which sits BELOW the deps layer and therefore catches a module that imports src/lib/db.js's shared client directly and never looks at deps; (2) pg.Client/Pool.prototype.query, with an SQL classifier (classifyStatement, exported and unit-tested) that separates reads, writes, control statements, DDL and the unclassifiable, refusing the last two outright. allow: [] is the default, so a table nobody named is refused. scan_runs and probe_tasks are the only tables openable at all (WRITABLE_BY_OPT_IN); scans, brand_metrics_daily and 18 other customer tables are in NEVER_WRITABLE and throw at install even if a test names them. An unknown .rpc() name is refused rather than assumed to be a reader. A refusal is recorded, printed to stderr and sets process.exitCode=1 with an exit-time summary, so insertScan's catch-and-cascade cannot swallow it into a green run. tasks.title: The live write guard cannot force its own adoption
tasks.detail: R3.2.4 built a default-deny write guard that stops a live test reaching a production write by omission, and proved it by writing the omitted-stub test and watching five writes refused. Its author then named the gap it cannot close: a live test that never calls installLiveWriteGuard is unprotected, and nothing makes a new file call it. A meta-test asserting every live-DB test file installs the guard would close it, but the repo has no naming convention to key on — probeTasksRace.test.mjs is a live file with no Live in its name. Two related items from the same author, worth the same pass. covers.supabase and covers.pg are the only thing standing between armed and theatre: if the dynamic import of pg or supabase-js failed the guard would look installed and refuse nothing. It warns loudly and leaves the flag false, and every live file asserts both — but that assertion is itself a convention a new file could omit, the same gap one level up. And the SQL classifier is a regex rather than a parser; one real hole was found and fixed mid-build, an UPDATE with a table alias read as a SELECT, and there may be others. The supabase-js path has no such weakness since it reads the table name directly.
tasks.accept: A live-DB test that does not install the guard fails a meta-test rather than running unprotected, and the covers assertion is enforced rather than conventional; both proven by adding a file that omits each and watching it fail.

tasks.title: On a refrozen scan, finalize summarizes engines that produced nothing and ignores the rows that exist
tasks.detail: Found and declared by the R3.2.5 implementer, who fixed the silence and then said plainly that the silence was not the whole defect. R3.2.5 makes a scan record say when its frozen engine set shrank or was refrozen, via summary_stats.engine_set_change. But runFinalizePhase summarizes only checkpoint.engines - the FROZEN list - so on a refrozen scan, where no frozen engine resolved and the run fell back to today's engine set, the rows the substituted engines actually produced are summarized by NOBODY. Every slice comes out empty and engines_counted is 0. That is data loss one step past R3.2.5's finding, and it makes the new record arguably worse than the old silence: the scan now says 'refrozen' while also reporting zero engines counted, so a reader could conclude the run produced nothing when in fact it produced results that finalize threw away. Fixing it changes scoring behaviour - which engines contribute to a headline blend - so it was correctly outside R3.2.5's accept.
tasks.accept: A refrozen scan summarizes the rows that actually exist rather than the frozen list that produced none, so engines_counted reflects real evidence; and the headline states plainly what set it was blended over, since a refrozen scan is not comparable to the frozen baseline. A test drives a full refreeze and fails if the produced rows are dropped or if engines_counted is 0 while probe rows exist.

tasks.title: A live test can spread process.env into the gate and bypass the write guard
tasks.detail: Found and PROVEN by the R3.2.4 round-three verifier, which wrote the offender and watched it write. R3.2.4 made arming the default-deny write guard a property of the gate: liveDbGate() throws when asked about the real process.env with a database configured and no guard armed, and a META assertion walks every importer of liveDbGate.js. Both mechanisms key on env === process.env. A caller that writes liveDbGate({ ...process.env }) gets a spread COPY, so the identity check is false and the gate opens. Measured: in a new live test run bare with credentials, the alias form (const env = process.env; liveDbGate(env)) THREW as designed, while the spread form OPENED the gate and the write SUCCEEDED to the recording server, exit 0, green - and the guard self-test stayed 21/21 with that offender sitting in the tree, because the META regex only matches liveDbGate() with an empty or literal process.env argument. Not failed on at the time because the escape hatch is genuinely needed (probeQueue.test.mjs and the guard self-test pass literal env objects) and spreading the real environment is a commission rather than the omission R3.2.4's accept names. But liveWriteGuard.js's own WHAT IT DOES NOT COVER list says an offender is a file that AVOIDS the gate, and this one ASKS it, so the caveat as written would mislead the next author.
tasks.accept: A live test that spreads or otherwise copies the real environment into the gate is either caught or explicitly documented as a bypass. The verifier's remedy: widen the META regex to flag any liveDbGate call whose argument text contains process.env, and add a sentence at liveDbGate.js:63-65 saying a spread of the real environment defeats the identity check. Proven by planting the spread-copy offender and watching the guard self-test fail rather than stay green.
