tasks.title: Content cost accumulates across rescues
tasks.detail: It currently overwrites, under-reporting spend on every rescue.
tasks.accept: A rescued content job's cost_total is the sum across attempts, not the last attempt.

notes.text: claimed

FINDING REPRODUCES. startContentJob built a fresh `stats = {cost:0}` per EXECUTION (contentWorker.js:155) and wrote `cost_total: round4(stats.cost)` at the two terminal writes, so a rescue (api/content/worker/route.js dispatchWithLease -> startContentJob(jobId,{leaseOwner})) replaced the recorded total with the last attempt's spend. Proven by execution, not by reading: with the accumulation mutated back to an overwrite the new test fails 0.04 !== 0.06 on a job that really cost both attempts.

WHAT CHANGED, and why it is two halves rather than one. (a) contentWorker.js:269 reads the row's recorded cost_total once per attempt into `costBase`; contentWorker.js:201 `costFields()` returns base + this execution's spend, so a rescue ADDS. The value written is ABSOLUTE, not a delta, which is what makes re-writing it many times per attempt incapable of double-counting. (b) contentWorker.js:248 puts costFields() on EVERY job write, not just the terminal one. This half is load-bearing and the accept criterion is not met without it: the ONLY way a content job becomes rescuable is CONTENT_JOB_RUNNING status + stale heartbeat + free lease (db/content.js shouldRescueContentJob), i.e. a worker that was KILLED and never reached a terminal write at all. A fix that only accumulates at the end would have been green on a naive test and worth nothing in production, because attempt 1 would have recorded nothing to accumulate onto. Folding per block boundary leaves a killed attempt's real spend on the row. Residual loss window: spend inside the block that was in flight when the process died.

NO DOUBLE COUNT, structurally: absolute writes mean the success write and a subsequent catch write put the same number. A retried attempt that was already recorded is in costBase and is never re-added — the base is read once, before any spend. An attempt that fails before spending adds 0.

NOT AN ATOMIC INCREMENT, stated explicitly as the task asked: the storage layer does not offer one. supabase-js has no `cost_total = cost_total + $1` expression and content_jobs has no RPC (claim_scan_job_attempt / increment_scan_rate_limit are SQL functions on other tables). This is a read-modify-write with the read at attempt start. It is safe today because the job lease makes two executions of one job structurally impossible and reviseContentItem (contentWorker.js:616, which already accumulated — that path was NOT the bug) only folds into awaiting_approval jobs, which are not rescuable. A zombie that lost its lease and kept running can still lose an update. An atomic increment RPC would need a migration plus edits to src/lib/db/content.js and src/lib/liveWriteGuard.js, all outside my file scope — filed for the controller rather than done here. NO MIGRATION IS NEEDED for this fix: cost_total already exists (002_content_os.sql:14).

RULE 1 / RULE 5: when the job row was never read (a failure at or before getContentJob) the field is OMITTED from the failure write rather than written as 0 — a 0 there would erase an earlier attempt's spend, and we do not know the prior total. Tested at contentWorker.test.mjs:826. A cost_total that is present but unparseable logs a named warning (contentWorker.js:262) instead of silently becoming 0.

TESTS, with teeth proven by two mutations, each applied and then restored (sha256 verified identical to pre-mutation, no git checkout/stash used). Mutation A (drop costBase, i.e. the old overwrite): 4 red including 'the job cost both attempts and the row must say so 0.04 !== 0.06'. Mutation B (keep costBase but fold only at the terminal write): 3 red including 'a killed attempt must leave its spend on the row 0 !== 0.02'. The rescue test runs TWO attempts on ONE mutable row, attempt 1 abandoned mid-Writer via a never-settling LLM promise (the closest in-process model of a killed worker), attempt 2 the rescue, and asserts 0.06 = 0.02 + 0.04 AND asserts it is not 0.04.

SUITE: npm run test:scoring 2202 tests / 2176 pass / 0 fail / 26 skipped, twice in a row. Baseline given to me was 2147/2118/3 fail (landingHonesty) — those three are now fixed by another agent and the count grew because other agents are adding tests to this tree concurrently. One intermediate run reported 2 failures I could not reproduce on four subsequent runs and could not name (no assertion text in the output); I attribute it to another agent writing a file mid-run, not to this change. contentWorker.test.mjs alone: 21/21.

BE SUSPICIOUS OF: (1) cost_total is now written on every job update instead of only at the end, so the Studio theater shows a running cost mid-job and /api/content/[job_id]/status can return a non-final total — I judge that honest and an improvement, but it is a visible behaviour change. (2) the read-modify-write window described above. (3) I did NOT touch the cost cap: assertUnderCostCap still measures THIS execution's stats, so a rescued job can still spend up to CONTENT_MAX_COST_PER_ITEM again and the job's true total can exceed the cap N times over. Now that the row carries an honest total that cap could read it — deliberately left alone as beyond this accept criterion, and it wants its own task.

FILES: only src/lib/content/contentWorker.js and src/lib/content/contentWorker.test.mjs. Nothing outside src/lib/content/. Nothing staged or committed. Both files were also converted back to LF — my editor had rewritten them wholesale to CRLF, which .gitattributes (eol=lf) forbids; the committed diff is 267 insertions / 4 deletions across the two files, not a whole-file rewrite.

SECRETS: no credential value printed. Searches were git grep or src/-scoped only; no recursive search from the repo root, no .env file read.

Anchor :28-29 is the missing-key throw, unrelated to pricing; no change made there.

The one case that cannot be decided pre-flight is an unknown OpenRouter id, which is allowed through because usage.include is supposed to answer for it -- if the echo does not arrive, resolveCost throws after the fact rather than inventing a zero (llmPricing.js:258). Both throw UnpricedModelError and log '[llm-price] UNPRICED MODEL' (llmPricing.js:212). NO SILENT /usr/bin/bash REMAINS on this path: cost now comes from exactly one of three named sources and carries the name back as cost_source -- 'gateway' (real echoed spend), 'free_tier' (:free suffix), 'price_table' (tokens x rate). There is no fourth branch; anything else throws. A gateway-reported 0.0 stays 'gateway' (a measurement); a priced model with zero/absent tokens is 'price_table' 0 and does NOT throw; a :free id is 'free_tier'. usage.cost must ARRIVE as a number/numeric string -- Number(null) is 0, so a coerce-first check would have reintroduced the same bug wearing a mask (llmPricing.js:270-276).

tasks.title: openai.js has the identical dead retry guard perplexity just fixed, so a 401 costs three calls and three seconds
tasks.detail: Found by the R2.2.10 implementer after fixing the same bug in perplexity.js, and confirmed by execution there: a status-based retry guard sits above a throw whose enclosing catch backs off and loops regardless of status, so the guard is dead code. src/lib/engines/openai.js:59 and :124 have the same shape. R2.2.10 exported the fix as reusable units - classifyHttpStatus, failureKindOf and isRetryableFailure in perplexity.js - and noted that brightdata.js:408 already discriminates correctly and was the pattern it followed. The right move is to lift the classification into a shared module rather than copy it a third time. Note the deliberate asymmetry R2.2.10 chose and documented: an unreadable status defaults to TRANSIENT, because giving up early on a failure we cannot classify discards a measurement, which is the worse error. Keep that decision rather than re-litigating it. Test by counting invocations of an injected fetch stub, never by asserting on a log line, and never make a real API call.
tasks.accept: A 401 from openai costs exactly one call; a 500 keeps the full retry budget; both proven by counting calls to an injected fetch stub. The classification is shared with perplexity rather than duplicated. Deleting the retryability check turns the call-count tests red.

tasks.title: Firecrawl degrade becomes a recorded state
tasks.detail: The literal string 'No website content available.' can currently be fed to prompt generation as if it were site content.
tasks.accept: A Firecrawl degrade records its state on the scan and can never enter a prompt as content; a test asserts the string never reaches prompt generation.

notes.text: claimed

FINDING REPRODUCED AT HEAD (8502166), fetch stubbed, no network, in a throwaway git worktree since removed. Firecrawl stubbed to 402 (the real no-balance response) and the site refusing the connection: scrapeForSummary returned the literal "No website content available."; that exact string appeared in 1 of 1 LLM prompts under the heading "Website summary:"; the SERP seed miner derived the terms [website,website,content,content,available,available] from it and sent them to PAA/autocomplete as real Google queries; and stats after the run was {cost:0,tokens:0} - no record of the degrade anywhere. The same script on the fixed tree: 0 of 1 prompts contain the sentinel, the "Website summary:" heading is absent entirely, seed terms are [], and stats.website_scrape = {state:unavailable, state_reason:fallback_request_failed, reasons:[firecrawl_http_error,fallback_request_failed], detail:ECONNREFUSED, content_chars:0}.

WHAT CHANGED. The sentinel WAS the content channel; that is the bug, so it stopped being a return value. scrapeForSummary(url)->string is GONE, replaced by scrapeSite(url, deps) -> {content: string|null, content_chars, state, state_reason, reasons[], detail, source, degraded} (firecrawl.js:144). Three states, following R2.1.1's state+state_reason convention rather than inventing one: ok (Firecrawl gave usable content), degraded (content exists but came from the crude HTML strip, never from the vendor), unavailable (content is null). Ten reason tokens (firecrawl.js:35-66): no_url, unusable_target, firecrawl_not_configured, firecrawl_http_error, firecrawl_request_failed, firecrawl_thin_content, fallback_http_error, fallback_request_failed, fallback_empty_body, plus two legacy tokens for injected string scrapers. reasons[] keeps the whole chain, so a vendor 402 followed by a dead socket reports BOTH and the first is not erased by the second. fallback_empty_body vs fallback_request_failed is deliberate rule-1 work: "we fetched and the page was blank" is a measured nothing and must not look like "we never got a response".

NO PATH INVENTS ok. summarizeScrape(null) returns state=unavailable/no_scrape_result with content_chars NULL, not 0 - zero would claim we measured the content (rule 5); a real unavailable scrape reports content_chars 0, and both are asserted, paired, in the tests.

FIVE CALLERS, all converted. I found two of them only after a test failure, then re-grepped exhaustively; there are no others. promptGen.js: the snippet assignment now goes through sanitizeWebsiteSnippet (promptGen.js:61,225), which collapses null/blank/the sentinel to empty, and buildGenPrompt omits the "Website summary:" heading entirely when there is nothing, because an empty labelled block is itself a claim that we read the site. prompts.js:43. knowledge/route.js:82 - the 422 now names scrape_state and scrape_state_reason instead of collapsing every failure into one sentence, and a degraded-but-stored block gets its own warn. content/steps/research.js:43. Both knowledge/route.js and research.js were STRING-COMPARING against the sentinel to detect failure - the sentence was literally the API - and both now read the state.

BELT AND BRACES: normalizeScrapeResult (firecrawl.js:343) coerces an injected legacy string scraper into the envelope and recognises the sentinel as "there was nothing", so the string cannot reach a prompt even from an un-migrated caller. Six already-committed tests inject a scrape dep that returns the sentinel verbatim, and pass unchanged through it.

Also fixed while in the file: FIRECRAWL_API_KEY was captured at module load, so no test could exercise both the keyed and unkeyed paths in one process. It is read per call now and accepts deps.apiKey.

THE HALF I DID NOT CLOSE, PLAINLY. "Records its state ON THE SCAN" is NOT fully done and I am not claiming it is. promptGen writes the state to stats.website_scrape (promptGen.js:262), the mutable accumulator the worker already threads through this call. runSourcingPhase in src/lib/workers/scanWorker.js:897 copies only {cost, tokens} out of that object into the checkpoint, so website_scrape stops there and never reaches scan_runs.detail. I was instructed not to touch scanWorker.js - another implementer is in it right now, and it is currently BROKEN in the tree: scanChunkLedger.test.mjs imports recordEngineResolutionSkip, which exists neither at HEAD nor in the worktree. The missing hop is three lines: add WEBSITE_SCRAPE_DEGRADED to CHUNK_SKIP_REASONS (scanWorker.js:189); call recordSkip(tally, that reason, state_reason) in runSourcingPhase when stats.website_scrape.state is not ok; carry website_scrape into the phase return at :897 alongside prompt_source. No migration needed - it rides scan_runs.detail like every other skip. The gap is written into the code at promptGen.js:250-259 so a reader cannot miss it. Until it lands the degrade is loud in logs and recorded in-process, but not durable.

21 NEW TESTS in src/lib/firecrawlDegradeState.test.mjs, every fetch stubbed and every DNS lookup injected: the healthy path (asserts the vendor call is NOT followed by a site fetch); all five degrade paths table-driven (no key, 402, 500, thrown/timeout, thin content), each asserting state=degraded plus its own reason plus source=fallback_fetch; both-paths-dead with the two-reason chain; the blank-page measured-empty; a sweep that no outcome returns the sentinel; summarizeScrape's null-vs-zero pair; and the accept criterion three ways - through the new envelope, through a LEGACY string scraper returning the sentinel verbatim, and through the seed-term miner. Plus a test that a HEALTHY scrape still reaches the prompt (the fix must not blind the generator) and that a clean read emits NO degrade warning, so "degraded" is not just always-on.

tasks.title: Seven IPv6 ranges classifyAddress still allows
tasks.detail: R3.7.1 verifier enumerated the IPv6 space against the shipped classifier and found seven ranges that pass: fec0::/10 (deprecated site-local), 64:ff9b:1::/48 (local-use NAT64), ::ffff:0:0/96, 2001:2::/48 (BMWG benchmarking), 3fff::/20, 5f00::/16, and 2001:10::/28 (deprecated ORCHID). But a host resolving into one of these is not a public internet address either, and the module presents itself as a complete classifier. Cheap to close since the CIDR table already exists.

notes.text: claimed

ALL THREE ACCEPT CLAUSES MET AND RUN AGAINST THE LIVE DATABASE. Records what it applied: schema_migrations (filename, checksum, applied_at) is created first and written inside each file's transaction; the live table now holds all nine rows with checksums. Transaction per file: BEGIN / apply / record / COMMIT with ROLLBACK on failure, so a migration that dies halfway no longer leaves a schema no file describes for the next run to layer over. Reports a DB missing 006 as incomplete: the verify list stopped at 005 and now covers 001-009 keyed BY MIGRATION FILE, checked against the catalog, printing INCOMPLETE and setting exit 1 on any miss. Verified live: all 24 expected objects across 9 migrations tick, exit 0. THIS IS THE TOOL THAT FAILED TODAY, so two details are deliberate. The old runner printed 'Migrations applied successfully.' BEFORE verifying — the sentence that made a broken run look fine; success is now claimed only after the check, and a test asserts that string cannot return. And function existence is checked via pg_proc, not to_regclass, because 009 was found this morning with its TABLE present and its increment_scan_rate_limit FUNCTION absent — a to_regclass-only check would have passed on exactly that state. Also added: a checksum mismatch warns that a migration was edited after being applied, so the file no longer describes the database. GUARD IS AGAINST STALENESS, not against today's list: it walks supabase/migrations and fails if any file lacks an entry, and also fails on an entry for a file that no longer exists. TEETH: deleting the 006 entry — the literal C10 shape — fails 2 of 6.

rejected: REJECTED on evidence integrity and on the regression guard. THE IMPLEMENTATION IS GENUINELY GOOD AND ALL THREE ACCEPT CLAUSES HOLD BEHAVIOURALLY — the verifier proved that themselves. DO NOT REWRITE scripts/setup-supabase.mjs's logic.

WHAT IS VERIFIED. The original failure was reproduced: the old runner against a DB missing 006-009's objects printed "Migrations applied successfully." plus 17 ticks and exit 0; the new runner on the identical stub state prints 6 crosses, INCOMPLETE and exit 1. Clause 2 was proven properly, with a stub pg client and a full query log: BEGIN, migration body, INSERT INTO schema_migrations, COMMIT are ALL TAGGED THE SAME TRANSACTION ID, so the recording is genuinely inside the apply's transaction rather than adjacent to it; and a mid-file failure gives BEGIN, throw, ROLLBACK in the same transaction with no INSERT, no COMMIT, exit 1, and later migrations not attempted. Clause 3 exercised against a stubbed catalog omitting 006's sentinel: INCOMPLETE, exit 1. The verifier also reproduced the exact 2026-08-30 state — 009's table present, its function absent — giving a tick for the table and a cross for the function. THE pg_proc CATCH IS REAL AND CONFIRMED ON LIVE PROD: to_regclass returns NULL for increment_scan_rate_limit while pg_proc finds it, so a to_regclass-only check literally cannot see that function. Good catch, correctly implemented. THE GUARD WALKS: dropping a new migration file in makes it fail NAMING the file, and deleting the 006 entry from EXPECTED_OBJECTS fails 2 of 6 as claimed. schema_migrations holds 9 rows with real checksums that match the implementer's checkout byte for byte.

WHY IT FAILS.

(1) TWO OF THREE EVIDENCE CITATIONS POINT AT UNCHANGED, UNRELATED LINES. setup-supabase.mjs:16 is "import pg from 'pg';" — pre-existing, untouched by the commit; the added import is createHash on line 15. setup-supabase.mjs:112 is "if (process.env.SUPABASE_DB_HOST) {" — pre-existing connection-string plumbing, unrelated to the ledger, the transaction or the verify list. Only :40 lands inside the change, and it is a prose comment rather than the mechanism. Standing rule 6 exists so a citation proves where the change lives.

(2) THE REGRESSION GUARD CANNOT DETECT THE FAILURE IT EXISTS TO PREVENT. All six tests in src/lib/migrationsLedger.test.mjs are REGEXES OVER THE RUNNER'S SOURCE TEXT; nothing ever executes it. The verifier changed the failure branch to exitCode 0 and parked a dead "if (false) process.exitCode = 1;" in the success branch. The runner then PRINTED INCOMPLETE AND EXITED 0 ON A DB MISSING 006 — the literal C10 false success — and PASSED 6 OF 6 GUARDS. A syntactically broken runner that fails node --check also passes 6 of 6. assert.match(src, /INCOMPLETE/) checks the spelling of the criterion, not the criterion. This is the tool that failed on the day it was written; its own reliability is the thing under test.

(3) THE PREMATURE-SUCCESS ORDERING IS NOT PINNED. The test bans one literal string. Restoring "Migrations applied successfully" correctly fails 1 test, so that half of the note is true. But putting a DIFFERENT success sentence in the same pre-verification slot passes 6 of 6. Separately, setup-supabase.mjs:179 still prints "Migrations applied." before verification, so "success is claimed only after the check" is softer than stated — though the INCOMPLETE text does explicitly disclaim it, which is a deliberate mitigation.

(4) THE CHECKSUM LEDGER IS LINE-ENDING SENSITIVE AND SELF-ERASING. 001 and 006 are CRLF in the main tree and LF in any fresh, Linux or CI checkout, so running setup:db from an LF checkout warns that files nobody edited have CHANGED — and then the ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE SET checksum at :165-170 OVERWRITES the recorded checksum. The drift signal fires exactly once and destroys its own evidence; the next run is silent. The column records what the last checkout looked like, not what was applied. This compounds R6.4.7, the mixed-line-endings task.

TO FIX: (a) repoint the three evidence lines at the ledger DDL, the transaction block and the INCOMPLETE branch. (b) Add a BEHAVIOURAL test that imports the runner with a stubbed pg — module.registerHooks mapping the "pg" specifier to a virtual module exporting a fake Client works cleanly on Node 26 and takes about 90 lines — asserting exitCode 1 when the catalog omits 006, that the ledger INSERT falls between BEGIN and COMMIT, and that a throwing body produces ROLLBACK with no INSERT. (c) Either assert the ordering positionally (indexOf of any success sentence greater than indexOf of the verify loop) or drop the ordering claim from the note. (d) Normalise line endings before hashing, or hash the parsed statements, and decide whether an upsert that erases drift is the behaviour you want.

tasks.title: Agents grep secrets into transcripts; the exclusion must be in the brief, not the discipline
tasks.detail: Two verifiers on R0.1.6 leaked credentials into their transcripts by running unscoped greps that matched .env.local — one printed most of a retired MiMo key, the other a full GSC service-account private key (R0.1.15). Both disclosed it themselves, which is the system working, but the second happened AFTER the first was reported, which is the system not learning. The rule currently lives in whatever the controller remembers to type into each prompt. It belongs in the agent definitions under .claude/agents/ so every rebuild-verifier, rebuild-implementer, rebuild-surveyor and rebuild-scribe carries it by construction: never print a credential value, and always pass --exclude='.env*' (or an equivalent path filter) to any recursive search. A repo-level guard is worth considering too — a test asserting no tracked file contains a private-key header would not catch a transcript leak, but a .gitignore check and a documented grep idiom would reduce the surface. Standing rule 9: a change to the orchestration tooling is itself ledger work.
tasks.accept: Every rebuild-* agent definition carries the never-print-a-credential rule and the --exclude='.env*' idiom; a fresh agent spawned from each definition can quote the rule back without being told it in its prompt.

tasks.title: The checksum drift warning asserts a schema mismatch that may not exist
tasks.detail: scripts/setup-supabase.mjs hashes the whole migration file after normalising line endings and trailing whitespace, but NOT comment text. So a comment-only edit changes the checksum and the runner prints 'The file no longer describes what is in the database.' R1.2.2 produced exactly this: correcting a false header comment in 010_probe_tasks.sql moved the hash from be27ae10f9467429 to ed5bc223145c0461 while the deployed SQL was verified byte-identical, 232 non-comment lines unchanged. The warning is therefore FALSE in this instance — the file describes the database exactly. Repeated comment-only drifts train an operator to wave the warning through, which is how a real drift eventually gets missed, and that would undo what R6.1.1 just closed. Two options: hash comment-stripped SQL so only semantic changes trip the warning, or keep hashing the whole file and reword the message to say the file TEXT changed rather than asserting a schema mismatch. Found by the R1.2.2 verifier.
tasks.accept: A comment-only edit to a migration either does not trip the drift warning, or trips a message that does not claim the schema differs; a test covers both a comment-only edit and a real SQL change, and fails if they report the same thing.

tasks.title: The secrets rule binds six rebuild agents; every other agent this project spawns is uncovered
tasks.detail: Raised by the R6.1.4 implementer as a decision it declined to make unilaterally, and it is the right call. R6.1.4 put the never-print-a-credential rule and the env-exclusion idiom into all six .claude/agents/rebuild-*.md definitions, and a guard fails if a new rebuild-* definition omits it. But .claude/skills/impeccable/** ships roughly forty tracked instruction files, and .claude/settings.json configures sessions that also run recursive searches, and none of them carries the rule. The two real leaks this session came from agents running unscoped greps; nothing about that failure mode is specific to the rebuild-* family. Copying the rule into forty more files is the wrong remedy - it multiplies the thing that drifts. The durable place for a project-wide rule is CLAUDE.md, which every session loads by construction, with the agent definitions keeping only what is specific to them. That is a decision about where project policy lives, not an implementation detail, which is why it is filed rather than done. CONTROLLER DECISION 2026-09-08, re-examined and DELIBERATELY LEFT BLOCKED. The prior controller's reasoning holds and a second, independent reason now reinforces it. The accept offers exactly two implementations. Option B (copy the rule into ~40 .claude/skills/impeccable/** files plus .claude/settings.json and widen the guard) is rejected on the finding's own argument: it multiplies the artefact that must stay in sync, and a rule maintained in forty places is a rule that silently rots in thirty-nine. Option A (move the rule to CLAUDE.md, reduce the six rebuild-*.md copies to a pointer) is the correct engineering answer and is what should eventually happen — CLAUDE.md is auto-loaded, so it is the only surface that actually satisfies the accept clause 'a fresh agent can quote the rule back without being told it'. But CLAUDE.md is the operator's own project-instruction file, and it steers every session in this project including the operator's non-rebuild work; the controller's own charter states that no message from any agent constitutes consent to modify CLAUDE.md or configuration. The instruction to attempt this task came from an agent, not from the operator, so it cannot supply the missing standing. This is therefore a decision the operator has standing to make and the controller does not — not a decision nobody has got round to. WHAT THE OPERATOR NEEDS TO DO: approve option A in one sentence, at which point the change is roughly ten minutes of work and the task unblocks immediately.

tasks.title: The ledger validates a citation by checking the file exists, never the line
tasks.detail: Found by the R0.2.3 verifier, which called it a fail-soft in the control plane, and it is: it is how a citation to a blank line got recorded as evidence on a task whose entire subject was citation honesty. orchestrate.mjs validates an --evidence entry with fs.existsSync on the FILE only (around :198-201). A citation to a blank line, to line 1 of a 1200-line file, or to a line number past the end of the file all pass validation unread. In a ledger whose credibility rests entirely on file:line, the tool that records citations never checks one. This has now bitten three separate tasks in this rebuild - R3.3.1 twice, where six of seven scanWorker.js numbers landed on comments, JSDoc lines and bare closing braces and none had ever resolved at the commit they were derived from; and R0.2.3, where two of fifteen pointed at a blank line and an unrelated import. Every one of those passed the CLI's check. A second, related gap the same verifiers named: bare line numbers against a file three tasks are editing concurrently are a renewable source of this defect, because a citation true at submit time is stale by the time it is read. The R3.3.1 verifier measured 13 of 19 citations going stale in the working tree within one session.
tasks.accept: The CLI refuses an evidence citation whose line number exceeds the file's line count or resolves to a blank line, and says which citation and why. Evidence may optionally pin a commit (path:line@ref) for files under concurrent edit, and a pinned citation is resolved at that commit rather than at the working tree. Proven by submitting a citation to a blank line and to a past-the-end line and watching each be refused by name.

tasks.title: orchestrate.mjs takes the submit note as a shell argument, so backticks in a note execute and write command output into the ledger
tasks.detail: Hit independently by TWO implementers in the same round (R2.8.12 and R2.10.2), which makes it systematic rather than careless. A submit note is free prose and will naturally contain backticks around identifiers and file paths. Passed as a double-quoted bash argument, the shell performs command substitution BEFORE orchestrate.mjs ever sees the string. R2.8.12 lost six code snippets. R2.10.2 lost three spans AND had `git status --porcelain -- src/` actually EXECUTE, injecting an unrelated list of other agents modified files into the middle of a sentence in the permanent ledger note. No credential was involved in either case, but nothing about the mechanism prevents one: any command an agent quotes in prose is run with the agent full shell privileges and its stdout is written verbatim into tasks.json. That is a ledger-integrity bug and a latent disclosure path, not a style nit. The R2.10.2 implementer also correctly identified why the obvious repair is wrong: amend appends its note text to the task detail field, which is the spec other agents read, so using amend to fix a mangled submit note pollutes the specification. The two defects compound.
tasks.accept: A submit or amend note cannot be mangled or executed by the shell. Either the note is read from a file or stdin rather than argv, or the CLI documents and the agent definitions mandate a heredoc, with a guard that fails if an agent definition omits it. A test feeds a note containing backticks, a dollar-parenthesis substitution and a newline, and asserts the stored note is byte-identical to the input. Separately, amend gains a way to correct a note without appending to detail.

tasks.title: A NUL byte in a source file makes it invisible to every grep-based guard
tasks.detail: Found by the R0.1.18 implementer, who accidentally introduced one. While editing src/lib/rateLimit.test.mjs a stray NUL byte landed in the file; the file then read as binary rather than UTF-8 to file(1) and to ripgrep, which SILENTLY SKIPS binary files rather than erroring. The implementer noticed and removed it, so no NUL is in the tree today. The hazard it exposes is structural and is not specific to that file: this repo's guard strategy leans heavily on grep-based walkers (the route-perimeter walker, the engine-name walker, the doc-to-source staleness tripwire, checkSecrets' vendor-set comparison, the types.test.mjs env-var scan). Every one of them proves a property by finding or not finding text. A file containing a NUL is skipped without a message, so a guard that scans for a forbidden pattern reports a clean pass over a file it never opened. That is the same shape as the R6.3.1 finding where a conclusion was reached by checking one of two surfaces: the walker is not wrong, it is blind, and blindness reads as success.
tasks.accept: A NUL byte anywhere in a tracked text source file fails a test, naming the file. The guard itself must not be grep-based, since that is the exact tool being defeated. Proven by planting a NUL in a source file and watching the guard name it, then removing it.

tasks.title: A JSX apostrophe opens a phantom string literal in every comment-stripping guard in the repo
tasks.detail: Two independent verifiers (R6.4.9 and R2.7.10) reproduced the same root class against unmodified source, so this is a repo-wide sweep, not a single-file fix. Every comment-stripping scanner here treats a single quote as a JS string opener. JSX text is not JS, and the guarded files are JSX, so one apostrophe in rendered prose shifts quote-pairing phase and the remainder of the line - or of the file - is misread. Separately 5 non-test files ALREADY have a genuine line comment survive stripping: src/lib/db/analytics.js, src/lib/db/content.js, src/lib/prompts.js, src/lib/scoring/enginePipeline.js, src/lib/scoring/promptGen.js. The exploit needs no artificial setup: inserting one commented-out import between DashboardShell.jsx:362 and :364 - inside the pre-existing phantom string span, adding no quote character - made routeReachability go 10 pass / 0 fail while an orphan component sat unreached. R6.4.9 and R2.7.10 each close it in their own file; this task finds every other guard that shares the shape.

CLAUSE 1: full suite 974 pass / 0 fail WITH the real BRIGHTDATA_API_KEY exported ambiently, and keyless, and via npm run test:scoring with the guard's diagnostic visibly printing "set (len 36)" so the run is demonstrably not vacuous. serp.test.mjs is 7/0 in all three configs — keyless, key ambient, and key with SERP_PROVIDER=brightdata forced.

CLAUSE 2 VERIFIED INDEPENDENTLY OF THE FILE'S OWN GUARD, which is the right way to check a guard. The verifier wrote an out-of-band observer that snapshots the four vars, dynamically imports serp.test.mjs, and prints from process.on('exit') — after every test and every hook. All four vars come back strictly === their start values, keyed and keyless. Identity comparison on the real strings rules out a same-length substitute.

FIVE SABOTAGES, NONE OF THEM EDITING serp.test.mjs — each was a generated sibling copy outside the *.test.mjs glob, with the transform asserting non-no-op and printing the mutated region. S1 reverting the :65/:72 ordering reproduces the round-1 defect byte for byte: 6/1 with "started set (len 36), ended set (len 10)" and the observer confirming identical=false. S2 dropping BRIGHTDATA_API_KEY from SERP_ENV gives 3/4 keyed and 6/1 keyless, matching the claim exactly. S3 neutering useSerpEnv's restore catches the SERPAPI_KEY mock-key leak. S5 restoring a SAME-LENGTH fake ('X'.repeat(36)) still fails with "holding a different value" — the guard is not fooled by a fabricated credential of the right shape.

THE ORDERING MECHANISM WAS VERIFIED, NOT ASSUMED: a separate probe established that node:test runs top-level tests sequentially in registration order, runs t.after hooks in registration order, and completes all of test N's hooks before test N+1's body — so :246 observes the true post-hook state of everything above it.

THE APPEND-BELOW-:246 FRAGILITY IS REAL AND WAS DEMONSTRATED: S4 appends a leaking test below the guard and the file reports 8/0 GREEN while the observer shows SERPAPI_KEY leaking. Accepted here because it is coverage decay rather than runtime false-success — the guard cannot lie, it can only stop looking — the accept does not ask for position independence, and :247-255 warns future editors. The immune version was verified to work and costs nothing: a file-scoped after() imported from node:test, registered anywhere, runs after EVERY test in the file including appended ones, and node:test reports the thrown assertion as a file-level failure. Filed as a follow-up.

ONE CORRECTION TO THE IMPLEMENTER'S REASONING, right conclusion by the wrong mechanism: the note claims the keyless bite for the round-1 bug comes from the SERPAPI_KEY/mock-key path. Measured, it does not — under the ordering bug useSerpEnv's hook still deletes SERPAPI_KEY correctly. The true keyless bite is stronger: BRIGHTDATA_API_KEY goes unset -> 'bd-ambient', i.e. the file CONJURES A CREDENTIAL FROM NOTHING, which is the more serious shape.

LENGTH DISCLOSURE JUDGED CORRECT TO KEEP: it is load-bearing, not incidental. "started set (len 36), ended set (len 10)" is what makes the failure diagnosable; a bare "set" would render the round-1 defect as "started set, ended set", which reads like a nothing-burger. The equal-length case is already covered without disclosure by the "holding a different value" suffix, and check-secrets.mjs:268 is a real precedent whose citation resolves.

Branch-var enumeration re-confirmed as three (SERP_PROVIDER, BRIGHTDATA_API_KEY via brightdata.js:7, SERPAPI_KEY via resolveSerpCredentials) with BRIGHTDATA_SERP_ZONE a harmless superset; and no module in the import graph writes process.env at load, so PROCESS_START_ENV really is the inherited environment. Scope clean: commit 99e6060 is one file, test-only, +47/-2. Worktree verified pristine afterwards by sha256 against the committed file.

tasks.title: gemini.js abort signal never reaches the SDK
tasks.detail: src/lib/gemini.js:46 passes { requestOptions } where the @google/generative-ai SDK expects requestOptions directly. Confirmed twice by direct SDK comparison at version 0.24.1: with the shipped shape the fetch init keys are method, headers, body and there is NO signal; with the correct nesting the keys include signal. So the AbortController is inert and Promise.race is the only timeout — the request is abandoned, not cancelled, and up to 15 in-flight requests from the five-model fallback ladder can outlive the call that started them. On the long-lived worker in R1.2 that is a socket and quota leak rather than a slow request. Found by the R6.3.1 scribe while documenting the vendor and independently reproduced by its verifier.
tasks.accept: The abort signal reaches the SDK's fetch, proven by asserting the init object carries signal; an aborted call stops the upstream request rather than merely abandoning it, and a test fails if the argument shape regresses.

notes.text: filed mid-rebuild
claimed

gemini.js:56 now passes requestOptions DIRECTLY (was: model.generateContent(prompt, { requestOptions })). Reproduced BEFORE fixing: with the shipped shape the fetch init keys were exactly [body, headers, method] with no signal, and all 15 ladder requests were still live at return; the test file run against unfixed gemini.js failed 4/6 with exactly that evidence. After the fix the init carries a signal and the ladder failure changed from 'Gemini timeout' (abandoned) to GoogleGenerativeAIAbortError 'Request aborted when fetching ...' (cancelled). Cancellation vs abandonment proven three ways: the stub's signal fires abort exactly once per attempt, the stub fetch rejects AbortError, and the SDK surfaces the abort error. Note SDK 0.24.1 relays the caller signal through its OWN internal controller, so identity is impossible by construction; the test asserts linkage (init.signal !== ours AND aborts when ours does) and asserts init.signal !== undefined under a requestOptions that carries NO timeout, so a signal there can only have come from the call's controller. gemini.js:55 drops the SDK 'timeout' field on purpose: buildFetchOptions schedules a setTimeout(abort) it never clears, stranding one timer per rung (measured via process.getActiveResourcesInfo) - the same leak, moved. gemini.js:92-94 adds a finally that clears both deadlines and aborts the rung before the ladder advances. Regression guard at geminiAbort.test.mjs:155 asserts arg.requestOptions === undefined and arg.signal instanceof AbortSignal, captured by wrapping GoogleGenerativeAI.prototype.getGenerativeModel. Sabotage battery, 5 mutations, each proven applied: re-wrap => 4 fails; drop clearTimeout(timeoutId) => 2 fails; drop clearTimeout(raceTimeoutId) => 2 fails; re-add SDK timeout => 3 fails; drop controller.abort() from finally => 0 fails, disclosed in the code comment at gemini.js:88-91 as belt-and-braces rather than test-proven, because today the abort deadline and the race deadline fire at the same instant. No live vendor calls: globalThis.fetch stubbed in all 8 tests, GEMINI_API_KEY overwritten with a fake, no --env-file. npm run test:scoring: 1057 tests, 1047 pass, 1 fail, 9 skipped; the single failure is docStatus.test.mjs 'README migration table lists every migration on disk' over the untracked supabase/migrations/011_scan_runs.sql from a concurrent implementer, not mine. verification.note:
VERIFIED by an independent agent with its own harness, not the implementer's tests. REPRODUCED at the true pre-fix commit ee5504e~1 (the verifier corrected my brief): stubbing globalThis.fetch, the init keys were body/headers/method with signal UNDEFINED, and after a 20s deadline 5 of 5 ladder requests were STILL LIVE with zero abort events. At HEAD the same harness gives signal present, 0 of 5 live, and 5 abort events. With retries=2, 15 of 15 are torn down.

SIGNAL IDENTITY: the note's claim that object identity is impossible is TRUE and was verified in the SDK source rather than taken on trust — @google/generative-ai/dist/index.mjs:439-454 builds its OWN AbortController and relays via addEventListener, so the caller's signal object can never appear on the init. The tests do not settle for presence: substituting a foreign, never-aborted AbortSignal — which satisfies "an AbortSignal is present" and passes the flat-shape guard — FAILS 3 tests. Linkage is distinguished from presence.

CANCELLATION, NOT ABANDONMENT, on three independent observations: the stub's signal fires abort once per attempt; the fetch rejects with an AbortError so the chain terminates; and the SDK surfaces GoogleGenerativeAIAbortError instead of the old "Gemini timeout", which is exactly the change of error identity that distinguishes the two. The residual limit is honest and unavoidable — real socket teardown is undici's behaviour on init.signal and no stub can prove it; the mechanism reaching undici is proven correct.

A SECOND LEAK WAS FOUND AND CLOSED BY THE IMPLEMENTER ON THEIR OWN: clearTimeout ran only on the success path and the race timer was never cleared at all. The finally block clears both, measured via process.getActiveResourcesInfo as 0 pending Timeout resources after a 5-rung failure. Dropping the SDK's own timeout field is justified rather than a shortcut — the SDK schedules setTimeout(abort) and NEVER clears it, which would strand one timer per rung, relocating the leak.

SIX SABOTAGES, each diff-proven applied: the shipped { requestOptions } shape fails 4; a full revert fails 6 of 8; the foreign signal fails 3; re-adding the SDK timeout fails 3; dropping clearTimeout fails 2; dropping controller.abort() from finally fails 0 — the implementer's own disclosure, and accurate: the abort deadline timer is registered before the race timer with the same delay so Node fires abort first, making that line belt-and-braces today. It is disclosed in the code rather than dressed up as test-proven, which is the honest handling.

SDK VERSION: 0.24.1 installed, declared as a caret range and not pinned, though the lockfile resolves deterministically for npm ci. The implementer gets credit they did not claim — geminiAbort.test.mjs:97 and :124 pin the SDK's OWN behaviour, asserting the wrapper shape yields no signal and the flat shape does, so a version bump that flipped the argument shape fails loudly rather than silently reinstating an inert controller. The assumption is executable, not documentary.

LIVENESS rebuilt: POST /api/opportunities is served by Next regardless of in-repo callers and sits behind the operator perimeter, so it is reachable by any authenticated operator client; its only shipped browser caller has zero importers, and the other three importers of gemini.js are dead. The leak was real but currently unexercised. Suite 1106/1087/0/19, no live vendor call, main repo never written to.

TWO STALE FIGURES IN THE NOTE, neither a false claim about the shipped code: "failed 4/6" matches no configuration at HEAD (a full revert fails 6 of 8, the isolated re-wrap 4 of 8; the figure describes an intermediate draft), and the quoted suite count predates the 011 commit.

FOLLOW-UP FILED, and it is a direct consequence of this fix landing: docs/vendors/gemini.md now asserts a fixed bug as current — its quirk 3 heading says the SDK never receives the signal, its contract row says the timeout is enforced by Promise.race only, and every citation in that section now resolves to unrelated code. No test guards vendor-doc citations, so the suite will not catch it. The implementer was right not to widen the diff into a governed doc.

tasks.title: liveWriteGuard.test.mjs:290 passes alone and fails in the full run
tasks.detail: Reported independently by two implementers this session (R3.7.7's and R0.1.16's), each while trying to establish whether their own change had broken anything. The test named 'uninstall really restores both prototypes' at src/lib/liveWriteGuard.test.mjs:290 PASSES in isolation and FAILS in the full npm run test:scoring run, and it fails with the reporting file removed from the tree, so it is not caused by either of their changes. The mechanism is almost certainly shared mutable state: liveWriteGuard patches SupabaseClient.prototype and pg.Client/Pool.prototype, and the node test runner puts several files in the same worker process, so another file that installs or fails to uninstall the guard leaves the prototypes in a state this assertion does not expect. This matters more than an ordinary flake because the file under test IS the harness that decides whether a live test can write to production. A guard whose own self-test depends on which siblings share its worker is not evidence about the guard. Note this interacts with R3.2.4's rework, which is adding a --import preload that arms the guard for EVERY test file; that preload will change what the prototypes look like at the moment this assertion runs.
tasks.accept: The test's verdict does not depend on which other files share its worker process: it passes in isolation and in the full suite, and the invariant it asserts is established by construction (explicit setup/teardown or process isolation) rather than by luck of ordering. Proven by running it both ways, repeatedly, and by demonstrating the specific cross-file interaction that made it fail.

tasks.detail: Reported by the R3.2.6 implementer, who had to refactor around it to make its own acceptance criterion exercisable at all. tasks.title: An assert.equal on a credential env var prints the live value into CI logs when it fails
tasks.detail: Found by the R6.5.5 verifier in adjacent pre-existing code it was not asked to change, and correctly reported rather than fixed. src/lib/engines/serp.test.mjs uses assert.equal(process.env.BRIGHTDATA_API_KEY, undefined, ...) to assert that an ambient key did not survive the env scrub. node:test prints the actual value in its error dump EVEN WHEN a custom message is supplied - the verifier confirmed this in an isolated repro using a sentinel, not a real value. So on any machine where BRIGHTDATA_API_KEY is genuinely set, a regression in the scrub makes the test reporter print the live key into the CI log. The assertion that exists to prove a credential was cleared is the thing that would disclose it. This session has already had two real key leaks from agent transcripts; this is the same failure mode wired into the suite itself.
tasks.accept: No assertion anywhere in the suite can print a credential value on failure. The fix pattern is assert.ok(process.env.X === undefined, msg) - the boolean collapses actual to false - matching the describeEnv shape-only convention R6.5.5 established. A guard walks the test tree and fails on assert.equal / assert.strictEqual / deepEqual whose first argument reads a known-credential env var.

It does NOT follow a value through a local: 'const k = process.env.SOME_KEY; assert.equal(k, ...)' leaks identically on failure - node:test prints actual twice even with a custom message - and reads completely clean to the guard. That is one line of refactoring away from being reintroduced, in the exact file family the guard was written for. Two real credentials have already leaked into agent transcripts this session, so the cost of the gap is established rather than hypothetical. The fix shape is a choice worth stating: either follow single-assignment locals within a test body, or invert the rule and require that any assertion touching a secret-shaped name go through the existing shape-only describeEnv helper, which is checkable without dataflow.
tasks.accept: A test that reads a secret-shaped env var into a local and asserts on it is refused. A committed fixture holds that exact shape and the guard is asserted to reject it. The guard still does not fire on an assertion about a non-secret variable, proved by a near-miss fixture.
